## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Abhidhammatthasaṅgaho
## Ganthārambhakathā
Having respectfully paid homage to the Incomparable Fully Enlightened Buddha, together with the Sublime Dhamma and the Noble Saṅgha, I shall speak the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha, which is a summary of the meanings taught in the seven books of the Abhidhamma.

## Catu-paramattha-dhamma
In that Abhidhamma, the meanings taught are, in the ultimate sense, fourfold in every way: consciousness (citta), mental factors (cetasika), matter (rūpa), and Nibbāna.

3. Among those (four ultimate realities), consciousness is first fourfold: sense-sphere consciousness, fine-material-sphere consciousness, immaterial-sphere consciousness, and supramundane consciousness.

4. Among those (four types of consciousness), what is sense-sphere consciousness?

One consciousness accompanied by joy, associated with wrong view, unprompted; one prompted.

One consciousness accompanied by joy, dissociated from wrong view, unprompted; one prompted.

One consciousness accompanied by equanimity, associated with wrong view, unprompted; one prompted.

One consciousness accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from wrong view, unprompted; one prompted.

These eight are called greed-rooted consciousnesses.

4. Among those (four types of consciousness), what is sense-sphere consciousness?

## Summary of Enumeration of Consciousness

Unwholesome consciousness are thus twelve,
Wholesome consciousness are twenty-one;
Resultant consciousness are thirty-six,
Functional consciousness are twenty.

In the sense-sphere, fifty-four types,
In the fine-material-sphere, fifteen are taught;
In the immaterial-sphere, consciousness are twelve,
Likewise, in the supramundane, there are eight.

Thus, the consciousness which is of eighty-nine types,
Or otherwise, of one hundred and twenty-one types,
The wise divide (and distinguish).

## 2. Compendium of Mental Factors
## Characteristics of Association

Those states which arise together with consciousness, cease together with it,
Which have the same object and the same base as consciousness,
And which are associated with consciousness,
Are known as the fifty-two mental factors.

## Ethically Variable Mental Factors

How? These seven mental factors—contact, feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness, life-faculty, and attention—are called Universals (common to all consciousness).

These six mental factors—initial application, sustained application, decision, energy, zest, and desire—are called Occasionals.
20:
Thus, these thirteen mental factors should be known as the 'Common-to-each-other' (aññasamāna) mental factors.

## Unwholesome Mental Factors

Moha (delusion), ahirika (shamelessness), anottappa (fearlessness of wrongdoing), uddhacca (restlessness), lobha (greed), diṭṭhi (wrong view), māna (conceit), dosa (hatred), issā (envy), macchariya (stinginess), kukkucca (remorse), thina (sloth), middha (torpor), and vicikicchā (doubt)—these fourteen mental factors are called unwholesome mental factors.

## Beautiful Mental Factors

Saddhā (faith), sati (mindfulness), hirī (shame), ottappa (fear of wrongdoing), alobha (non-greed), adosa (non-hatred), tatramajjhattatā (equanimity), kāyapassaddhi (tranquillity of mental body), cittapassaddhi (tranquillity of consciousness), kāyalahutā (lightness of mental body), cittalahutā (lightness of consciousness), kāyamudutā (malleability of mental body), cittamudutā (malleability of consciousness), kāyakammaññatā (wieldiness of mental body), cittakammaññatā (wieldiness of consciousness), kāyapāguññatā (proficiency of mental body), cittapāguññatā (proficiency of consciousness), kāyujukatā (rectitude of mental body), and cittujukatā (rectitude of consciousness)—these nineteen...

These three mental factors, namely: Sammāvācā (right speech), Sammākammanta (right action), and Sammā-ājīva (right livelihood), are called the Virati (Abstinence) mental factors. These mental factors, namely: Karuṇā (compassion) and Muditā (appreciative joy), are called the Appamaññā (Illimitable) mental factors. ## Method of Association

Of those mental factors which are always associated with consciousness,
Following this brief summary,
In each thought-arising (or in each consciousness),
Association is stated in detail according to their appropriate combinations.

Seven (universals) are associated with all (consciousness),
The miscellaneous factors are associated as appropriate.
Fourteen (unwholesome factors) are associated only with unwholesome consciousness,
The beautiful factors are associated only with beautiful consciousness (as appropriate).

## Method of Association of Common-to-each-other Mental Factors

How do they associate? Firstly, regarding the seven universal mental factors (sabbacittasādhāraṇa): these seven universal mental factors are obtained in all eighty-nine types of thought-arising.
23: Among the miscellaneous (pakiṇṇaka) mental factors, firstly, the Vitakka (initial application) mental factor arises in fifty-five types of consciousness, namely: the forty-four sense-sphere consciousness (kāmāvacara-citta) excluding the ten-fold sense-consciousness (dve-pañca-viññāṇa), and the eleven first jhāna consciousness. The Vicāra (sustained application) mental factor arises in sixty-six types of consciousness, namely: those fifty-five associated with Vitakka and the eleven second jhāna consciousness. The Adhimokkha (decision) mental factor arises in all consciousness excluding the ten-fold sense-consciousness and the consciousness accompanied by doubt (vicikicchā). The Vīriya (energy) mental factor arises in all consciousness excluding the five-door adverting (pañcadvārāvajjana), the ten-fold sense-consciousness, the receiving (sampaṭicchanna), and the investigating (santīraṇa) consciousness. The Pīti (rapture) mental factor arises in all consciousness excluding those accompanied by displeasure (domanassa), those accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā), the two types of body-consciousness (kāyaviññāṇa), and the fourth jhāna consciousness. The Chanda (desire-to-act) mental factor arises in all consciousness excluding the rootless (ahetuka) and the delusion-rooted (mohamūla) consciousness.

## Method of Association of Unwholesome Mental Factors

Among unwholesome types of consciousness, these four mental factors—moha (delusion), ahirika (shamelessness), anottappa (fearlessness of wrongdoing), and uddhacca (restlessness)—are called universal unwholesome factors (sabbākusalasādhāraṇa); they are obtained in all twelve unwholesome types of consciousness.

Lobha (greed) is obtained only in the eight types of consciousness rooted in greed.
25: The Diṭṭhi (wrong view) mental factor is obtained in the four consciousness associated with wrong view (diṭṭhigatasampayutta). The Māna (conceit) mental factor is obtained in the four consciousness dissociated from wrong view (diṭṭhigatavippayutta). These four mental factors—Dosa (hatred), Issā (envy), Macchariya (avarice), and Kukkucca (worry)—are obtained in the two types of consciousness associated with aversion (paṭighasampayutta). The Thina-middha (sloth and torpor) mental factors are obtained in the five prompted (sasaṅkhārika) consciousness. The Vicikicchā (doubt) mental factor is obtained only in the consciousness accompanied by doubt (vicikicchāsahagata). Four factors in all unwholesome consciousness, Three are found in greed-rooted consciousness. Four in the hate-rooted consciousness, Likewise two in the prompted consciousness. In the doubt-accompanied consciousness, there is Vicikicchā. Thus, these fourteen unwholesome mental factors Associate only with the twelve unwholesome consciousness In five distinct ways.

Likewise, in the determining consciousness (votthabbana), (11 ethically variable mental factors), excluding desire and zest, (enter into the combination).

In the investigating consciousness accompanied by joy (somanassa-santīraṇa), (11 ethically variable mental factors), excluding desire and effort (viriya), (enter into the combination).

In the ten types of sense-consciousness (dvipañcavijñāṇa), it should be understood that only those seven (universal) mental factors are included, excluding the particulars (pakiṇṇaka).

In all eighteen rootless consciousnesses, the inclusion (sangaha) occurs in four ways by way of counting.

Twelve, eleven, ten, and seven—thus the fourfold method of inclusion in the eighteen rootless consciousnesses should be understood.

In all rootless consciousnesses, the seven (universal) mental factors are associated; the remaining (particular) mental factors are associated as appropriate. Thus, the 33-fold inclusion has been explained in detail.

Having thus understood the method of association (sampayoga-naya) and the method of inclusion (sangaha-naya) of the mental factors associated with consciousness, one should demonstrate the various ways in which they are associated with consciousness as appropriate.

In the Abhidhammattha Sangaha, the second part called the Analysis of Mental Factors (Cetasika-sangaha-vibhāga) is finished.

## 3. Miscellaneous Section (Pakiṇṇaka-pariccheda)
The states of consciousness and mental factors are associated together as appropriate. In their own nature, they are of fifty-three kinds. Now, I shall explain the sixfold miscellaneous inclusion (pakiṇṇaka-sangaha) called the inclusion of feeling, etc., by way of the arising of consciousness as appropriate, through the distinctions of feeling (vedanā), root (hetu), function (kicca), door (dvāra), object (ālambaṇa), and base (vatthu). ## Inclusion of Feeling (Vedanā-sangaha)
Among those six miscellaneous inclusions, in the inclusion of feeling, first, feeling is of three kinds: pleasant (sukha), painful (dukkha), and neither-painful-nor-pleasant (adukkhamasukha). Furthermore, by way of distinction, it is fivefold: pleasure (sukha), pain (dukkha), joy (somanassa), displeasure (domanassa), and equanimity (upekkhā).
40: In that inclusion of feeling, the consciousness accompanied by pleasure (sukha) is only one: the wholesome-resultant body-consciousness (kusalavipāka kāyaviññāṇa). Similarly, the consciousness accompanied by pain (dukkha) is only one: the unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness (akusalavipāka kāyaviññāṇa). The types of consciousness accompanied by joy (somanassa) are sixty-two: namely, the eighteen types of sense-sphere joy-accompanied consciousness—four rooted in greed (lobhamūla), twelve sense-sphere beautiful (kāmāvacara-sobhana) consciousnesses, and two (rootless) being joy-accompanied investigating (sukha-santīraṇa) and smile-producing (hasituppāda) consciousnesses—and the forty-four types of sublime (mahaggata) and supramundane (lokuttara) consciousnesses known as the first, second, third, and fourth jhānas. The types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure (domanassa) are only the two types of consciousness associated with aversion (paṭigha-sampayutta). All the remaining fifty-five types of consciousness are accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā).

(Continued from the previous page) ...are only the two types of consciousness associated with aversion.

7. It should be understood that all the remaining fifty-five types of consciousness, excluding those accompanied by pleasure, pain, joy, and displeasure, are only those accompanied by equanimity.

8. In that inclusion of feeling, feeling is of three kinds by way of the characteristic of experiencing: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and equanimity feeling. By way of the distinction of joy and displeasure, it is fivefold.

9. Pleasant feeling and painful feeling are each established in one type of consciousness. Displeasure is established in a group of two types of consciousness. Joy is established in sixty-two types of consciousness. The remaining equanimity is established in fifty-five types of consciousness. The inclusion of feeling is finished.

## Inclusion of Roots (Hetu-sangaha)
10. In the inclusion of roots, the so-called roots are of six kinds: greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), delusion (moha), non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), and non-delusion (amoha).

11. In that inclusion of roots, five-door adverting (pañcadvārāvajjana), the ten types of sense-consciousness (dvipañcavijñāṇa), receiving (sampaṭicchana), investigating (santīraṇa), determining (voṭṭhabbana), smile-producing (hasana)—
42:
—by way of these, eighteen types of consciousness are named rootless (ahetuka).

12. All the remaining seventy-one types of consciousness, excluding the eighteen rootless ones, are named rooted (sahetuka) because they have associated roots.

13. Among those seventy-one rooted consciousnesses, the two types of consciousness rooted in delusion (mohamūla) are named single-rooted (ekahetuka) because they have only one root.

14. The ten types of unwholesome consciousness excluding the two rooted in delusion, and the twelve sense-sphere beautiful consciousnesses that are dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta)—these twenty-two types of consciousness are named double-rooted (dvihetuka) because they have two roots.

15. It should be understood that the twelve sense-sphere beautiful consciousnesses associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayutta), and the thirty-five sublime and supramundane consciousnesses—these forty-seven types of consciousness are named triple-rooted (tihetuka) because they have three roots.

16. The three roots—greed, hatred, and delusion—are unwholesome roots. Non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are likewise wholesome roots and indeterminate (abyākata) roots.
43:
It should be understood that there are eighteen rootless consciousnesses, two single-rooted, twenty-two double-rooted, and forty-seven triple-rooted.

## Inclusion of Function (Kicca-sangaha)

In the inclusion of function, the so-called functions are of fourteen kinds: rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), life-continuum (bhavaṅga), adverting (āvajjana), seeing (dassana), hearing (savana), smelling (ghāyana), tasting (sāyana), touching (phusana), receiving (sampaṭicchana), investigating (santīraṇa), determining (vuṭṭhabbana), impulsion (javana), registration (tadārammaṇa), and death (cuti).

By way of the stages such as the rebirth-linking stage, life-continuum stage, adverting stage, fivefold sense-consciousness stage, etc., the distinction of the stages (ṭhāna) of those consciousnesses performing functions should be understood as being of ten kinds.

In that inclusion of function, the two types of investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity and the eight great resultants (mahāvipāka)...
44:
...and the nine fine-material and immaterial resultant consciousnesses—these nineteen types of consciousness are called those performing the functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death.

The consciousnesses performing the function of adverting are two.

Similarly, the consciousnesses performing the functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and receiving are (two each).

The consciousnesses performing the function of investigating are three.

Mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana) itself performs the function of determining (vuṭṭhabbana) in the five doors.

The fifty-five wholesome, unwholesome, fruition, and functional consciousnesses, excluding the two types of adverting, are those performing the function of impulsion (javana).

The eight great resultants and the three types of investigating consciousness—these eleven types of consciousness are called those performing the function of registration (tadārammaṇa).

Among those, the two types of investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity perform rebirth-linking, life-continuum...
45: ...death, registration, and investigation, and are thus called those performing five functions. The eight great resultants perform four functions by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, death, and registration. The nine sublime resultants perform three functions by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death. The investigating consciousness accompanied by joy performs two functions by way of investigation and registration. Similarly, the determining consciousness (vuṭṭhabbana) performs two functions by way of determining and adverting. All the remaining impulsion consciousnesses, the three elements of ideation (manodhātu), and the ten types of sense-consciousness (dvipañcavijñāṇa) perform only one function as appropriate.
46:
The consciousnesses have been shown as being of fourteen kinds by way of function, such as rebirth-linking and so forth, and of ten kinds by way of location. One should point out the consciousnesses that have one, two, three, four, and five functions and locations, being sixty-eight, two, nine, eight, and two in number respectively.

## Compendium of Doors
In the Compendium of Doors, what are called doors are of six kinds: the eye-door, the ear-door, the nose-door, the tongue-door, the body-door, and the mind-door.
47:
Among those six doors, the eye-sensitivity itself is called the eye-door. Likewise, the ear-sensitivity and so forth are called the ear-door and so forth. The mind-door, however, is called the life-continuum (the 19 types of bhavaṅgupaccheda).

Among those doors, in the eye-door, 46 types of consciousness arise as appropriate, by way of: five-door adverting, eye-consciousness (2), receiving (2), investigating (3), determining, sense-sphere javana (29), and registration (11).

Likewise, in the ear-door and so forth, 46 types of consciousness each arise by way of five-door adverting, ear-consciousness, and so forth. Thus, in all five doors, the consciousnesses that arise are only the 54 sense-sphere consciousnesses.

In the mind-door, however, 67 types of consciousness arise by way of mind-door adverting, 55 javanas, and 11 registrations.

The 19 types of consciousness that occur by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death are door-freed (dvāravimutta).
48:
Among those consciousnesses, the 10 sense-cognitions and the 26 sublime and supramundane javanas—making 36 in total—are called one-door consciousnesses (ekadvārika) as appropriate. 

The three mind-elements (manodhātu) occur in the five doors. 

Joyful investigation, determining (mind-door adverting), and the 29 sense-sphere javanas are six-door consciousnesses (chadvārika). 

The 2 types of equanimity-investigation and the 8 great resultants occur in the six doors and are also door-freed. 

The 9 sublime resultants are exclusively door-freed.

There are consciousnesses that occur in one door, those in five doors, those in six doors, those that occur in six doors and are door-freed, and those that are entirely door-freed.
49:
Thirty-six, likewise three, thirty-one in order, ten and nine—thus one should point out in five ways.

## Compendium of Objects (Ārammaṇa-saṅgaha)
In the Compendium of Objects, there are six kinds of objects, namely: visible object, sound object, smell object, taste object, tangible object, and mental object.

Among those six, visible form itself is called the visible object. Likewise, sound and so forth are called the sound object and so forth.

Mental objects, however, are classified into six kinds by way of: sensitive matter, subtle matter, consciousness, mental factors, Nibbāna, and concepts.
50:
In this Compendium of Objects, the object of all eye-door consciousnesses is the visible object alone, and that is only of the present. Likewise, the objects of ear-door consciousnesses and so forth are the sound object and so forth, and those are also only of the present.

The objects of mind-door consciousnesses, however, are all six kinds of objects, which occur as appropriate as present, past, future, or time-freed.

The objects of door-freed consciousnesses—known as rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death—are generally the six kinds of objects grasped in the previous existence through the six doors, being present, past, or concepts, and designated as Kamma, sign of Kamma (kamma-nimitta), or sign of destiny (gati-nimitta), as they may arise.

Among those, consciousnesses such as eye-consciousness and so forth have only one object each, such as visible object and so forth, in order.

The three mind-elements, however, have five objects, such as visible object and so forth.
51:
The remaining sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses and the smile-producing consciousness have only sense-sphere objects in every way. Unwholesome consciousnesses and sense-sphere javanas dissociated from knowledge have all objects except the supramundane. 

Sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses associated with knowledge and the wholesome direct-knowledge consciousness known as the fifth jhāna have all objects except the path and fruition of Arahantship. 

Sense-sphere functional consciousnesses associated with knowledge, functional direct-knowledge consciousness, and determining (mind-door adverting) consciousness have all objects in every way.

Among the immaterial-sphere consciousnesses, the second and fourth (the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception) have sublime objects. All other remaining sublime consciousnesses have concepts as objects. Supramundane consciousnesses have Nibbāna as their object.
52:
Twenty-five types of consciousness arise with respect to sense-sphere objects; six types of consciousness with respect to sublime objects; twenty-one types of consciousness with respect to concepts; eight types of consciousness with respect to Nibbāna. Twenty types of consciousness arise with respect to objects free from the supramundane; five types of consciousness arise with respect to all objects except the path and fruition of Arahantship; six types of consciousness arise with respect to all objects. Thus, in this Compendium of Objects, the classification is sevenfold.

## Compendium of Bases
In the Compendium of Bases, what are called bases are of six kinds: the eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, the tongue-base, the body-base, and the heart-base. All these bases are found in the sense-sphere.
53:
In the fine-material world, however, the three bases—nose, tongue, and body—do not exist. In the immaterial world, none of the physical bases exist at all.

In this Compendium of Bases, the five sense-cognition elements occur strictly depending on their respective five sensitive bases. The mind-elements, known as five-door adverting and receiving, occur depending only on the heart-base.

The remaining mind-consciousness elements—namely, the 3 investigating consciousnesses, 8 great resultants, 2 rooted in hatred, the path of stream-entry, the smile-producing consciousness, and the 15 fine-material sphere consciousnesses (30 in total)—occur depending only on the heart-base.

The remaining 12 mundane wholesome consciousnesses, 10 unwholesome consciousnesses (excluding the 2 rooted in hatred), 13 functional consciousnesses, and 7 supramundane consciousnesses (excluding the path of stream-entry), however, occur either depending on or not depending on (the heart-base).
54:
By way of immaterial resultants, it should be known that (mind-consciousness elements) occur without depending on the heart-base at all.

In the sense-world, seven elements of cognition occur depending on the six bases. In the fine-material world, four kinds (of cognition elements) occur (depending on three bases). In the immaterial world, one (mind-consciousness) element is known to occur without depending on any physical base.

Forty-three consciousnesses occur only depending (on a base); forty-two consciousnesses arise either depending on or not depending (on a base); and the immaterial resultants occur without depending (on a base).

## the Third Chapter in the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha.
55: ## 4. Vīthi-pariccheda (Analysis of Cognitive Processes) Having thus completed the excellent Summary of Miscellaneous Topics (Pakiṇṇaka-saṅgaha) which analyzes the four mental aggregates consisting of consciousness and mental factors, I shall now briefly explain, in all its variety and as it occurs, the Summary of the Occurrence of Consciousness (Pavatti-saṅgaha), also known as the Summary of Cognitive Processes (Vīthi-saṅgaha), which is distinguished by planes (bhūmi) and individuals (puggala), and is determined by the sequence of preceding and succeeding consciousness during rebirth and the course of existence. In the Summary of Cognitive Processes, six sets of six should be understood: six bases, six doors, six objects, sixfold consciousness, six processes, and the sixfold presentation of objects. However, for process-freed consciousness (vīthimutta), the presentation of objects is threefold by way of kamma, kamma-nimitta (sign of kamma), and gati-nimitta (sign of destiny).
56: Among those six sets of six, the bases, doors, and objects are exactly as previously explained. ## Viññāṇa-chakka (Sixfold Consciousness) There are six types of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. ## Vīthi-chakka (Sixfold Process) The six processes should be understood according to the sequence of consciousness occurring at the doors: either by way of the doors as the eye-door process, ear-door process, nose-door process, tongue-door process, body-door process, and mind-door process; or by way of consciousness as the eye-consciousness process, ear-consciousness process, nose-consciousness process, tongue-consciousness process, body-consciousness process, and mind-consciousness process.

## Sixfold Occurrence of Objects

It should be known that the occurrence of objects (visayappavatti) is sixfold: four in the five doors, namely: very great, great, slight, and very slight; and two in the mind-door, namely: clear and obscure.

## Five-door Process

How? The three sub-moments—arising, presence, and dissolution—constitute one thought-moment.

Seventeen such thought-moments are the lifespan of material phenomena.

Whether one thought-moment has passed or many thought-moments have passed, the five kinds of objects that have reached the stage of presence in the five doors...
58: They come into the focus of the door. Therefore, if a visible object that has passed for one thought-moment comes into the focus of the eye-sensitivity, then, after the life-continuum (bhavanga) has vibrated twice and the stream of bhavanga is cut off, a five-door adverting consciousness (pañcadvārāvajjana) arises and ceases, reflecting on that same visible object. Immediately after that, eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) seeing that same visible object, receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchanna), investigating consciousness (santīraṇa), and determining consciousness (votthapana/vuṭṭho) arise and cease in due order. Following the sequence of javana, two registration resultants (tadārammaṇa) occur as appropriate. After that, there is a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavanga).
59: To this extent, the 14 occurrences of process consciousness, 2 vibrations of bhavanga, and the 1 past thought-moment that occurred earlier, complete the 17 thought-moments. After that, the object ceases. This object is called a 'very great' (atimahanta) object. An object that comes into focus after several moments have passed, such that it is insufficient to last until the arising of registration (tadārammaṇa), is called a 'great' (mahanta) object. In that 'great' object process, there is only a lapse into bhavanga at the end of the javanas; registration does not arise. An object that comes into focus after several moments have passed, such that it is insufficient to last even until the arising of javana, is called a 'slight' (paritta) object. In that 'slight' object process, javana does not arise, and only the determining consciousness (votthapana) occurs two or three times. After that, there is only a lapse into bhavanga.
60: An object that comes into focus after several moments have passed, such that it is insufficient to last even until the arising of determining consciousness (votthapana), and is near its cessation, is called a 'very slight' (atiparitta) object. In that 'very slight' object process, there is only vibration of the bhavanga; no process consciousness arises. Thus, in the eye-door, and likewise in the ear-door and so on, the fourfold presentation of objects should be understood as the objects of the four courses (vāra) in the five doors, namely: the registration course, the javana course, the determining course, and the futile (mogha) course. There are only seven types of process consciousness. There are fourteen occurrences of consciousness. In detail, there are fifty-four types in the five doors as appropriate. ## This is the method of the occurrence of process consciousness in the five doors.

## Mind-door Process

## Process of Limited Javana

In the mind-door, if a clear object enters the range of the object, then after the vibration of the life-continuum, mind-door adverting, and javanas, the registration (tadārammaṇa) resultant consciousnesses occur; thereafter, there is a lapse into the life-continuum.

In the case of an obscure object, there is only a lapse into the life-continuum at the end of the javanas; it should be known that no registration occurs.

The process-thoughts are only three;
By way of thought-arisings (cittuppāda), ten are stated.
In detail, however, it should be understood that there are forty-one in this mind-door.

## This is the Process of Limited Javana (Sense-sphere Javana Process) in the mind-door.
62: ## Appanā-javana-vāra (Absorption Javana Course) In the Absorption Javana Course, there is no distinction between 'clear' and 'obscure' objects; likewise, registration (tadārammaṇa) does not arise. In this course, one of the eight sense-sphere javanas associated with knowledge arises four or three times in order, under the names of preparation (parikamma), access (upacāra), conformity (anuloma), and change-of-lineage (gotrabhu). Immediately after they cease, as the fourth or fifth moment, any one javana among the twenty-six sublime (mahaggata) or supramundane (lokuttara) javanas enters the absorption process according to the direction of the mind (abhinihāra). After that, at the end of the absorption javana, there is only a lapse into bhavanga. In that absorption course, it is expected that after a javana accompanied by joy (somanassa), the absorption will also be accompanied by joy; after a javana accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā), the absorption will also be accompanied by equanimity. In this javana course of similar feeling, after a wholesome javana, sublime and supramundane wholesome javanas and the three lower fruits occur by way of absorption. After a functional (kiriya) javana, functional javanas and the fruit of Arhatship occur.
63:
Immediately after the four sense-sphere javanas associated with knowledge and accompanied by joy, only absorption (appanā) accompanied by joy is expected. Immediately after the four sense-sphere javanas associated with knowledge and accompanied by equanimity, only absorption accompanied by equanimity is expected.

In that sequence of javanas with similar feeling, it should be understood that immediately after the four great wholesome javanas associated with knowledge, either a sublime or supramundane wholesome javana, or the group of the three lower fruition javanas, occurs by way of absorption. Immediately after the four great functional javanas associated with knowledge, either a sublime functional javana or the fruition javana of Arahantship occurs by way of absorption.

Following the two great wholesome javanas associated with knowledge and accompanied by joy, thirty-two types of absorption javanas arise.
Following the two great wholesome javanas associated with knowledge and accompanied by equanimity, twelve types of absorption javanas arise.
Following the two great functional javanas associated with knowledge and accompanied by joy, eight types of absorption javanas arise.
Following the two great functional javanas associated with knowledge and accompanied by equanimity, six types of absorption javanas arise.

Following the four sense-sphere wholesome javanas with three roots, forty-four types of absorption javanas arise for three-rooted worldlings and the three lower types of noble persons (learners).
Following the four sense-sphere functional javanas with three roots, fourteen types of absorption javanas arise for Arahants.

## This is the method of the occurrence of process-consciousness in the mind-door in this Compendium of Processes.

## The Law of Registration (Tadārammaṇa-niyama)

In this Compendium of Processes, in all five-door and mind-door processes, when the object is undesirable (aniṭṭha), the fivefold sense-consciousness, receiving, investigating, and registration are only unwholesome-resultants.

When the object is desirable (iṭṭha), the fivefold sense-consciousness, receiving, investigating, and registration are wholesome-resultants.

When the object is extremely desirable (ati-iṭṭha), however, the investigating and registration consciousnesses are only those accompanied by joy. Among those eleven types of registration, at the end of functional javanas accompanied by joy, only registration accompanied by joy occurs; at the end of functional javanas accompanied by equanimity, only registration accompanied by equanimity occurs.
65:
28. At the end of javanas accompanied by displeasure (domanassa), both registration and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) are only accompanied by equanimity. Therefore, if for a person whose rebirth-consciousness is accompanied by joy, registration does not occur at the end of javanas accompanied by displeasure, then teachers say that an investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity arises, taking as its object some previously familiar sense-sphere object; and immediately after that (adventitious life-continuum), the lapse into the life-continuum occurs.

29. Likewise, at the end of sense-sphere javanas, the occurrence of registration is expected only for sense-sphere beings and only regarding sense-sphere phenomena as objects.

30. It is said that registration occurs in the case of very distinct and great objects, when there is the fixed determination of javana, being, and object in the sense-sphere.

## The Law of Javanas (Javana-niyama)

31. Among javanas, in a sense-sphere javana process, the sense-sphere javanas run for seven times or only six times.

32. In the case of weak occurrence, such as at the time of death, etc., they run for only five times.

33. Teachers also say that for the Blessed One, at such times as the Twin Miracle, etc., because of the rapidity of occurrence, four or five moments of reviewing consciousness (paccavekkhaṇa) occur.

In the first absorption of a beginner, sublime javanas and direct-knowledge (abhiññā) javanas always run only once; after that, the lapse into the life-continuum occurs.

The arising of the four Paths lasts for only one mind-moment; after that, two or three moments of Fruition consciousness arise as appropriate; after that, the lapse into the life-continuum occurs.

At the time of the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), the fourth immaterial javana runs twice, and after that, one reaches cessation.

At the time of emerging from the attainment of cessation, either the Fruition of Non-returning or the Fruition of Arahantship arises once as appropriate, and after it has ceased, the lapse into the life-continuum occurs.

In all cases of the attainment process (samāpatti-vīthi), because there is no fixed law of the process as in the stream of the life-continuum, many javanas are obtained.

## Analysis of Persons (Puggala-bheda)

In this analysis of persons, those with two roots (duhetuka) and those with no roots (ahetuka) do not obtain functional javanas or absorption javanas.

Likewise, in a happy destination (sugati), they (those with two roots or no roots) do not obtain great resultant consciousnesses associated with knowledge.

In a woeful destination (duggati), however, (those with no roots) do not obtain great resultant consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge.

Among the nine types of three-rooted persons, Arahants do not obtain wholesome or unwholesome javanas.
69:
In the same way, learners (sekha) and worldlings (puthujjana) do not obtain functional javanas. Learners do not obtain javanas associated with wrong view or javanas accompanied by doubt. Non-returners (anāgāmi) do not obtain javanas of aversion (dosamūla). Supramundane javanas arise only for noble persons (ariya) as appropriate.

It should be shown that:
For Arahants, 44 process-consciousnesses arise;
For learners, 56 arise;
For the remaining worldlings, 54 arise,
as they are capable of occurring.

## This is the classification according to persons (Puggala-bheda) in this Compendium of Processes.

## Analysis of Planes (Bhūmi-vibhāga)

In the sense-sphere plane, all these process-consciousnesses are obtained as appropriate.

In the fine-material plane, process-consciousnesses are obtained excluding javanas of aversion and registration. In the immaterial plane, they are obtained excluding the Path of Stream-entry, fine-material sphere consciousness, the smile-producing consciousness (hasituppāda), and the lower immaterial consciousnesses. In all planes, those who lack a particular sensitivity (pasāda) do not obtain the process-consciousnesses belonging to that particular door. For non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), there is no occurrence of consciousness in any way at all.

In the sense-sphere plane, 80 process-consciousnesses,
In the fine-material plane, 64,
And likewise in the immaterial plane, 42,
are obtained as appropriate.

## This is the classification according to planes (Bhūmi-vibhāga) in this Compendium of Processes.

## 5. Compendium of Process-freed

In the manner already described, I have stated the Compendium of Occurrence (vīthi-sangaha) which occurs by way of process-consciousnesses. Now, I shall state the Compendium of Occurrence (vīthimutta-sangaha) which occurs at the time of rebirth-linking and death.

In the Compendium of Process-freed, four sets of four (tetrads) should be known: the four planes, the four types of rebirth-linking, the four types of kamma, and the four ways of the advent of death (maraṇuppatti).

## Tetrad of Planes

Among those four tetrads, there are four planes: the woeful plane (apāya-bhūmi), the sensuous blissful plane (kāmasugati-bhūmi), the fine-material-sphere plane (rūpāvacara-bhūmi), and the immaterial-sphere plane (arūpāvacara-bhūmi).
73:
Among those four planes, the woeful plane is fourfold: hell (niraya), the animal kingdom (tiracchāna-yoni), the sphere of petas (petti-visaya), and the host of asuras (asurakāya).

The sensuous blissful plane is sevenfold: the human realm (manussa), the realm of the Four Great Kings (cātumahārājikā), the realm of the Thirty-three (tāvatiṃsa), the realm of the Yāma gods, the Tusita realm, the realm of the gods who delight in creating (nimmānarati), and the realm of the gods who wield power over others' creations (paranimmitavasavatti).

These eleven planes together are known simply as the sensuous-sphere plane (kāmāvacara-bhūmi).

The first jhāna plane is threefold: the realm of the retinue of Brahmā (brahmapārisajja), the realm of the ministers of Brahmā (brahmapurohita), and the realm of the Great Brahmās (mahābrahmā).

The second jhāna plane is threefold: the realm of Minor Lustre (parittābha), the realm of Infinite Lustre (appamāṇābha), and the realm of Radiant Lustre (ābhassara).
74:
The third jhāna plane is threefold: the realm of Minor Aura (parittasubha), the realm of Infinite Aura (appamāṇasubha), and the realm of Steady Aura (subhakiṇha).

The fourth jhāna plane is sevenfold: the realm of Great Fruit (vehapphala), the realm of Non-percipient Beings (asaññasatta), and the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa). Thus, the fine-material-sphere plane is sixteenfold.

The Pure Abodes are fivefold: the Durable realm (avihā), the Serene realm (atappā), the Beautiful realm (sudassā), the Clear-sighted realm (sudassī), and the Highest realm (akaniṭṭhā).

The immaterial plane is fourfold: the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana-bhūmi), the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana-bhūmi), the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana-bhūmi), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-bhūmi).

In the Pure Abodes, worldlings (puthujjana) are not found at all,
nor are Stream-enterers (sotāpanna),
nor Once-returners (sakadāgāmi).
75:
Noble Ones (ariya) are not found in the realm of non-percipient beings or in the woeful planes. In the remaining places, both Noble Ones and non-Noble worldlings are found.

## This is the Tetrad of Planes in this Compendium of Process-freed.

## Tetrad of Rebirth-linking
Rebirth-linking is fourfold: woeful rebirth-linking, sensuous blissful rebirth-linking, fine-material-sphere rebirth-linking, and immaterial-sphere rebirth-linking.

Among those four types of rebirth-linking, the unwholesome-resultant investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity becomes the rebirth-linking at the moment of descent (rebirth-moment) in the woeful plane.
76:
After that rebirth-linking, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) occurs, and at the end, it ceases as death (cuti). This is called the single woeful rebirth-linking.

The wholesome-resultant investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity, however, occurs by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death for those in the sensuous blissful plane who are human beings, such as those blind from birth and so forth, and for the fallen asuras (vinipātikāsuras) who are dependent on the earth-dwelling deities.

The eight great resultants (mahāvipāka), however, occur by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death in all the sensuous blissful planes.

These nine types of rebirth-linking are called sensuous blissful rebirth-linking.

These ten types of rebirth-linking are collectively known as sensuous-sphere rebirth-linking (kāmāvacara-paṭisandhi).
77:
Among those beings (associated with the ten types of rebirth-linking), there is no fixed rule for the calculation of the lifespan of those in the four woeful planes, human beings, and fallen asuras.

The lifespan of the deities in the realm of the Four Great Kings is five hundred celestial years; in human calculation, it is nine million years. The lifespan of the Tāvatiṃsa deities is four times that of the Four Great Kings; the lifespan of the Yāma deities is four times that of the Tāvatiṃsa; the lifespan of the Tusita deities is four times that of the Yāma; the lifespan of the Nimmānarati deities is four times that of the Tusita; and the lifespan of the Paranimmitavasavatti deities is four times that of the Nimmānarati.

Nine hundred and twenty-one crores
of years, and likewise
sixty hundred-thousands (six million),
is the lifespan among the Vasavatti deities.
78:
The resultant consciousness of the first jhāna occurs by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death in the first jhāna plane.

Likewise, the resultant consciousness of the second jhāna and the resultant consciousness of the third jhāna occur in the second jhāna plane.

The resultant consciousness of the fourth jhāna occurs in the third jhāna plane.

The resultant consciousness of the fifth jhāna occurs in the fourth jhāna plane.

For non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), however, only matter (the vital nonad-kalāpa) becomes rebirth-linking. Likewise, after that rebirth-linking, during the course of existence and at the time of death, only matter occurs and then ceases. These are called the six types of fine-material-sphere rebirth-linking.

Among those beings (associated with the six types of rebirth-linking), the lifespan of the deities (Brahmās) born in the realm of the retinue of Brahmā (brahmapārisajja) is one-third of an aeon (kappa).
79: The lifespan of the Brahmās born in the realm of the ministers of Brahmā (brahmapurohita) is half an incalculable aeon (asaṅkhyeyyakappa). The lifespan of the Brahmās born in the realm of the Great Brahmās (mahābrahmā) is one incalculable aeon. The lifespan of the Brahmās born in the realm of Minor Lustre (parittābha) is two great aeons (mahākappa). The lifespan of the Brahmās born in the realm of Infinite Lustre (appamāṇābha) is four great aeons. The lifespan of the Brahmās born in the realm of Radiant Lustre (ābhassara) is eight great aeons. The lifespan of the Brahmās born in the realm of Minor Aura (parittasubha) is sixteen great aeons. The lifespan of the Brahmās born in the realm of Infinite Aura (appamāṇasubha) is thirty-two great aeons. The lifespan of the Brahmās born in the realm of Steady Aura (subhakiṇha) is sixty-four great aeons. The lifespan of the Brahmās born in the realm of Great Fruit (vehapphala) and the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) is five hundred great aeons. The lifespan of the Brahmās born in the Durable realm (avihā) is one thousand great aeons. The lifespan of the Brahmās born in the Serene realm (atappā) is two thousand great aeons. The lifespan of the Brahmās born in the Beautiful realm (sudassā) is four thousand great aeons. The lifespan of the Brahmās born in the Clear-sighted realm (sudassī) is eight thousand great aeons. The lifespan of the Brahmās born in the Highest realm (akaniṭṭhā) is sixteen thousand great aeons.
80: The resultant consciousnesses of the first immaterial sphere and so forth occur in the first immaterial plane and so forth respectively by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death. These four types of rebirth-linking are called immaterial-sphere rebirth-linking. Among those beings associated with these four types of rebirth-linking, the lifespan of the Brahmās who have reached the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana) is twenty thousand great aeons. The lifespan of the Brahmās who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) is forty thousand great aeons. The lifespan of the Brahmās who have reached the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) is sixty thousand great aeons. The lifespan of the Brahmās who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) is eighty-four thousand great aeons.
81:
Rebirth-linking consciousness, life-continuum consciousness, and likewise decease consciousness are of only one kind in a single existence (in terms of plane, type, associated states, and volitional activity). Likewise, they have the same object.

## This is the Fourfold Rebirth-linking (Paṭisandhi-catukka) in this context.

## The Fourfold Karma (Kamma-catukka)

There are four kinds of karma by way of function: Productive Karma (Janaka-kamma), Supportive Karma (Upatthambhaka-kamma), Obstructive Karma (Upapīḷaka-kamma), and Destructive Karma (Upaghātaka-kamma).

There are four kinds of karma by way of the order of ripening: Weighty Karma (Garuka-kamma), Death-proximate Karma (Āsanna-kamma), Habitual Karma (Āciṇṇa-kamma), and Reserve Karma (Kaṭattā-kamma).

There are four kinds of karma by way of the time of ripening: Immediately Effective Karma (Diṭṭhadhammavedanīya-kamma), Subsequently Effective Karma (Upapajjavedanīya-kamma), Indefinitely Effective Karma (Aparāpariyavedanīya-kamma), and Lapsed Karma (Ahosi-kamma).
82:
Likewise, there are four kinds of karma by way of the place of ripening: Unwholesome Karma (Akusala-kamma), Sense-sphere Wholesome Karma (Kāmāvacara-kusala-kamma), Fine-material-sphere Wholesome Karma (Rūpāvacara-kusala-kamma), and Immaterial-sphere Wholesome Karma (Arūpāvacara-kusala-kamma).

Among those four kinds of karma, Unwholesome Karma is threefold by way of the doors of action: Bodily Action (Kāya-kamma), Vocal Action (Vacī-kamma), and Mental Action (Mano-kamma).

How? The threefold action consisting of Killing (Pāṇātipāta), Stealing (Adinnādāna), and Sexual Misconduct (Kāmesu micchācāra) is called Bodily Action because it occurs mostly in the body-door, known as bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti).

That which is called False Speech (Musāvāda), Slandering (Pisuṇavācā), Harsh Speech (Pharusavācā), and Frivolous Talk (Samphappalāpa) —
83:
is called Vocal Action because it occurs mostly in the speech-door, known as vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti).

These three—Covetousness (Abhijjhā), Ill-will (Byāpāda), and Wrong View (Micchādiṭṭhi)—are called Mental Action because they occur mostly in the mind alone, even without intimation.

Among those (ten courses of unwholesome action), Killing, Harsh Speech, and Ill-will arise from the root of hatred (dosa-mūla). Sexual Misconduct, Covetousness, and Wrong View arise from the root of greed (lobha-mūla). The remaining four (Stealing, False Speech, Slandering, and Frivolous Talk) arise from both roots (greed and hatred).

By way of the arising of consciousness, however, this unwholesome karma is of twelve types in every respect.
84:
Sense-sphere Wholesome Karma is also threefold by way of the doors of action: Bodily Action occurring in the body-door, Vocal Action occurring in the speech-door, and Mental Action occurring in the mind-door.

Likewise, it is threefold by way of Giving (Dāna), Virtue (Sīla), and Meditation (Bhāvanā).

By way of the arising of consciousness, however, this (Sense-sphere Wholesome Karma) is of eight types.

It is of ten types by way of: Giving (Dāna), Virtue (Sīla), Meditation (Bhāvanā), Reverence (Apacāyana), Service (Veyyāvacca), Sharing of Merit (Pattidāna), Rejoicing in Merit (Pattānumodanā), Hearing the Dhamma (Dhammassavana), Teaching the Dhamma (Dhammadesanā), and Straightening of Views (Diṭṭhijukamma).

These twenty types (of wholesome and unwholesome karma) are reckoned simply as Sense-sphere Karma (Kāmāvacara-kamma).
85:
Fine-material-sphere Wholesome Karma is only mental action; it is born of meditation and has reached absorption (appanā). It is of five types according to the distinction of jhana factors.

Likewise, Immaterial-sphere Wholesome Karma is also mental action; it is also born of meditation and has reached absorption. It is of four types according to the distinction of objects.

Among these four kinds of karma, Unwholesome Karma, excluding restlessness (uddhacca), produces rebirth in the woeful planes (apāya-bhūmi). During the course of existence (pavatti), however, all twelve types of unwholesome karma produce seven unwholesome-resultant consciousnesses in the sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere in every respect as appropriate.

Sense-sphere Wholesome Karma also produces rebirth only in the sense-sphere fortunate planes (kāma-sugati-bhūmi), —
86:
and likewise, during the course of existence, it produces the Great Resultant consciousnesses (Mahā-vipāka). The eight rootless wholesome-resultant consciousnesses (ahetuka-kusala-vipāka), however, ripen in the sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere in every respect as appropriate.

Among those sense-sphere wholesome karmas, superior three-rooted (tihetuka-ukkaṭṭha) wholesome karma gives three-rooted rebirth and produces sixteen resultants during the course of existence.

Inferior three-rooted (tihetuka-omaka) wholesome karma and superior two-rooted (dvihetuka-ukkaṭṭha) wholesome karma give two-rooted rebirth and produce twelve resultants, excluding the three-rooted ones, during the course of existence.

Inferior two-rooted (dvihetuka-omaka) wholesome karma, however, gives only rootless rebirth and produces only rootless resultants during the course of existence.
87:
Some teachers say: 'Unprompted (asaṅkhārika) wholesome karma does not produce prompted (sasaṅkhārika) resultant consciousnesses, and prompted wholesome karma does not produce unprompted resultant consciousnesses.' In the view of those teachers, one should point out twelve, ten, and eight resultant consciousnesses respectively, according to the method already mentioned and as they arise.

If one develops the first jhana of the Fine-material-sphere Wholesome Karma to a limited degree, one is born in the realm of the Retinue of Brahma (Brahma-pārisajja).

Developing that same jhana to a medium degree, one is born in the realm of the Ministers of Brahma (Brahma-purohita).

Developing it to a superior degree, one is born in the realm of the Great Brahmas (Mahā-brahma).

Likewise, developing the second and third jhanas to a limited degree, one is born in the realm of Limited Radiance (Parittābha).
88:
Developing (the second and third jhanas) to a medium degree, one is born in the realm of Boundless Radiance (Appamāṇābha).

Developing them to a superior degree, one is born in the realm of Streaming Radiance (Ābhassara).

Developing the fourth jhana to a limited degree, one is born in the realm of Limited Lustre (Parittasubha).

Developing it to a medium degree, one is born in the realm of Boundless Lustre (Appamāṇasubha).

Developing it to a superior degree, one is born in the realm of Refulgent Lustre (Subhakiṇha).

Developing the fifth jhana, one is born in the realm of Great Reward (Vehapphala).

Developing that same fifth jhana with detachment from perception, one is born in the realm of Non-percipient Beings (Asaññasatta).

Non-returners (Anāgāmī), however, are born in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa).

It is said that if one develops Immaterial-sphere Wholesome Karma in due order, one is born in the Immaterial realms (Āruppa).
89:
Thus, Sublime (Mahaggata) merit, which is established according to the planes, produces a similar resultant at the time of rebirth and during the course of existence.

## This is the Fourfold Karma (Kamma-catukka) in this context of the Compendium of the Process-freed (Vīthimutta-saṅgaha).

## The Process of Decease and Rebirth (Cuti-paṭisandhi-kkama)

The occurrence of death (maraṇuppatti) is known to be of four kinds: through the exhaustion of the life-span (āyu-kkhaya), through the exhaustion of karma (kamma-kkhaya), through the exhaustion of both, and through the action of a destructive karma (upacchedaka-kamma).

To those beings who are thus dying, at the time of death, as appropriate, there appears at one of the six doors by the power of karma: either the karma that is to produce rebirth in the next existence; or a sign of karma (kamma-nimitta), which is an object such as a visible form previously obtained at the time of performing that karma and which serves as an instrument; or —
90:
a sign of destiny (gati-nimitta), which is to be obtained and experienced in the next existence. Thereafter, taking that very object which has appeared, the stream of consciousness—whether pure or defiled—flows repeatedly, mostly inclining towards the existence that is to be obtained, in accordance with the karma that is ripening.

Or else, that productive karma itself appears at the door by way of being newly performed.

To that being who is very close to death, at the end of the cognitive process (vīthi) or at the end of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the decease consciousness (cuti-citta), which is the final point of the present existence, arises and ceases by way of passing away.
91: When that decease-consciousness (cuti-citta) ceases, immediately after that decease-consciousness, taking the object as grasped [by the death-proximate impulsion], whether having a physical base or without a physical base as appropriate, the consciousness called rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) arises. It is produced by volitional formations (kamma) which are rooted in the latent tendency of craving (taṇhānusaya) and surrounded by the latent tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya). It is accompanied by its associated mental states, acts as the precursor by being the foundation for co-nascent states, and connects one existence to another. As soon as it arises, it establishes itself in the new existence. In this death-proximate process (maraṇāsanna-vīthi), however, only five impulsion (javana) moments, which occur slowly, are to be expected. Therefore, if death occurs while present objects that have come into range are still persisting, then the rebirth-linking and life-continuum (bhavanga) consciousnesses are also considered to be able to obtain a present object. Thus, in the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara)—
92: The rebirth-linking consciousness obtains a present or past object in the form of a sign of kamma (kamma-nimitta) or a sign of destiny (gati-nimitta) grasped through the six doors. Kamma, however, is exclusively past and is grasped only through the mind-door. All these objects are also of the limited (paritta/sense-sphere) nature. For fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) rebirth-linking, the object is only the sign of kamma which is a concept (paññatti). Similarly, for immaterial sphere (arūpa) rebirth-linking, the object is only the sign of kamma which is either sublime (mahaggata) or a concept, as appropriate. For the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), only the vital-nonad group (jīvita-navaka-kalāpa) is established as rebirth-linking. Therefore, they are called those with material rebirth-linking. Immaterial beings are those with mental rebirth-linking. The remaining beings are those with both material and mental rebirth-linking.
93:
After the four immaterial decease-consciousnesses (āruppa-cuti), the four immaterial rebirth-linkings (excluding the lower immaterial ones) and the four sense-sphere triple-rooted (kāma-tihetuka) rebirth-linkings occur. After the six fine-material sphere decease-consciousnesses, seventeen types of rebirth-linking occur, excluding the rootless (ahetu) ones. After the four sense-sphere triple-rooted decease-consciousnesses, all nineteen types of rebirth-linking occur. After the remaining two sense-sphere rootless decease-consciousnesses and four double-rooted decease-consciousnesses, only the ten sense-sphere rebirth-linkings occur in the eleven sense-sphere realms.

## This is the order of decease and rebirth-linking in this Compendium of Process-freed Consciousness.

For those who have thus obtained rebirth-linking, from the moment immediately after the cessation of the rebirth-linking consciousness, that same type of consciousness—taking that same object—continues to occur as the stream of life-continuum (bhavanga-santati) as a factor of existence, as long as no process-consciousness (vīthi-citta) arises, until the arising of the decease-consciousness. It flows incessantly like the current of a river.
94:
At the end, it becomes the decease-consciousness (cuti-citta) by way of deceasing and ceases. After that, rebirth-linking and so forth, revolving like a chariot wheel, continue to occur in due order.

Just as rebirth-linking, life-continuum, process-consciousnesses, and decease-consciousness revolve in this life, so too in another life, this stream of consciousness consisting of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and so forth, revolves again.

The wise, having reflected with wisdom upon this unstable round of existence, being of virtuous conduct, and having the bonds of affection well-severed by the Path, will reach the state of peace for a long time, having attained the deathless state (Nibbāna).

## Thus ends the fifth chapter, called the Compendium of Process-freed Consciousness,
## in the Abhidhammattha Sangaha.
95:
## 6. Rūpa-pariccheda (Analysis of Matter)
I have already explained the mental states—consciousness and mental factors—which have been analyzed by way of their varieties and occurrences through the five preceding chapters. Therefore, I shall now explain matter (rūpa) by way of its varieties.

In this Compendium of Matter, there is an enumeration by way of five aspects: enumeration (samuddesa), classification (vibhāga), origination (samuṭṭhāna), groups (kalāpa), and the mode of occurrence (pavattikkama).

## Rūpa-samuddesa (Enumeration of Matter)
Matter is of two kinds: the four great essentials (mahābhūta) and derived matter (upādā-rūpa) dependent on the four great essentials. These two kinds of matter are comprised under eleven categories.
96:
How are they enumerated? The earth element (pathavī-dhātu), the water element (āpo-dhātu), the fire element (tejo-dhātu), and the air element (vāyo-dhātu) are called essential matter (bhūta-rūpa).

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are called sensitive matter (pasāda-rūpa).

Visible form, sound, smell, taste, and tangible object—which consists of the three great essentials excluding the water element—are called objective matter (gocara-rūpa).

Femininity (itthibhāva) and masculinity (purisabhāva) are called gender matter (bhāva-rūpa).

The heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) is called heart matter (hadaya-rūpa).

The life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is called life matter (jīvita-rūpa).
97:
Edible food (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra) is called nutritive matter (āhara-rūpa).

Thus, these eighteen kinds of matter are comprised under the terms: matter with intrinsic nature (sabhāva-rūpa), matter with distinct characteristics (salakkhaṇa-rūpa), concretely produced matter (nipphanna-rūpa), matter as matter (rūpa-rūpa), and matter for comprehension (sammasana-rūpa).

The space element (ākāsa-dhātu) is called limiting matter (pariccheda-rūpa).

Bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti) and vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti) are called intimation matter (viññatti-rūpa).

Lightness of matter (lahutā), softness (mudutā), wieldiness (kammaññatā), and the two types of intimation matter are called mutable matter (vikāra-rūpa).
98:
Production (upacaya), continuity (santati), decay (jaratā), and impermanence (aniccatā) of matter are called characteristic matter (lakkhaṇa-rūpa).

Among these four characteristic matters, the single aspect of birth (jāti) is spoken of by the names production (upacaya) and continuity (santati). Thus, these eleven categories of matter consist of twenty-eight types by way of their own nature.

How is that?
Essential matter, sensitive matter, objective matter,
gender matter, heart matter,
life matter, and nutritive matter,
together make eighteen types (of concretely produced matter).
Furthermore, limiting matter, intimation matter,
mutable matter, and characteristic matter,
make ten types of non-concretely produced matter.
Thus, (matter) is of twenty-eight types.

## This is the enumeration of matter (Rūpa-samuddesa) in this Compendium of Matter.
99:
## Classification of Matter (Rūpa-vibhāga)

All this matter is rootless (ahetuka) [because it lacks associated roots], with conditions (sappaccaya) [because it has four causes], subject to taints (sāsava) [because it is an object of taints], conditioned (saṅkhata) [because it is produced by causes], mundane (lokiya) [because it is included in the world], belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) [because it is the range of sense-desire], without an object (anārammaṇa) [because it does not perceive objects], and not to be abandoned (appahātabba) [because it is not abandoned by the Path]. Thus, matter, which is of one kind in this way, is further divided into many types by way of internal (ajjhattika), external (bāhira), and so forth.

How is it divided? The five types of matter called sensitive matter (pasāda) are internal matter (ajjhattika-rūpa); the rest are external matter (bāhira-rūpa).

The six types of matter called sensitive matter and heart matter are base matter (vatthu-rūpa); the rest are non-base matter (avatthu-rūpa).

The seven types of matter called sensitive matter and intimation matter are door matter (dvāra-rūpa); the rest are non-door matter (advāra-rūpa).
100:
The eight kinds of matter, namely the 5 sensitive material qualities (pasāda-rūpa), 2 material qualities of sex (bhāva-rūpa), and 1 material quality of life (jīvita-rūpa), are called faculty-matter (indriya-rūpa). The remaining twenty kinds of matter are called non-faculty-matter (anindriya-rūpa).

The twelve kinds of matter, namely the 5 sensitive material qualities and 7 objective material qualities (visaya-rūpa), are called gross matter (oḷārika-rūpa), proximate matter (santike-rūpa), and impinging matter (sappaṭigha-rūpa). The remaining sixteen kinds of matter are called subtle matter (sukhuma-rūpa), distant matter (dūre-rūpa), and non-impinging matter (appaṭigha-rūpa).

Matter born of kamma is called acquired matter (upādinna-rūpa). The remaining matter is called unacquired matter (anupādinna-rūpa).

The visible form base (rūpāyatana) is called visible matter (sanidassana-rūpa). The remaining twenty-seven kinds of matter are called non-visible matter (anidassana-rūpa).
101:
The two kinds of matter starting with the eye (eye and ear), by way of not reaching the object, and the three kinds of matter starting with the nose (nose, tongue, and body), by way of reaching the object—these five kinds of matter are called field-grasping matter (gocaraggāhika-rūpa). The remaining twenty-three kinds of matter are called non-field-grasping matter (agocaraggāhika-rūpa).

The eight kinds of matter, namely color (vaṇṇa), odor (gandha), flavor (rasa), nutritive essence (ojā), and the four great elements (bhūta-rūpa), are called inseparable matter (avinibbhoga-rūpa). The remaining twenty kinds of matter are called separable matter (vinibbhoga-rūpa).

Thus, the wise analyze the twenty-eight kinds of matter appropriately, according to the divisions such as internal matter (ajjhattika-rūpa) and so forth.

## This is the Analysis of Matter (Rūpavibhāga) herein.
102:
## The Method of the Origins of Matter (Rūpasamuṭṭhānanaya)

The four things called kamma, consciousness (citta), temperature (utu), and nutriment (āhāra) are the causes that produce matter (rūpasamuṭṭhāna). Among these four causes, the twenty-five kinds of wholesome and unwholesome kamma, namely the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) kamma, produce kamma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa) in the internal continuity conditioned by them, at every moment starting from the arising moment (uppāda-khaṇa) of the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta). The seventy-five kinds of consciousness, excluding the four immaterial-sphere resultant (arūpa-vipāka) consciousnesses, the ten-fold sense-consciousness (dve-pañcavijñāṇa), and the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) of Arahants, produce consciousness-born matter (cittaja-rūpa) only at the arising moment, starting from the first life-continuum (paṭhama-bhavaṅga).
103: Among those seventy-five kinds of consciousness, the twenty-six kinds of absorption-impulsion (appanā-javana) also strengthen the bodily postures (iriyāpatha). Determining consciousness (vottthabbana), the thirty kinds of sense-sphere impulsion (kāma-javana), and the two kinds of direct-knowledge (abhiññā) also produce intimation (viññatti). Among those consciousnesses that produce intimation, the thirteen kinds of joyful impulsion (somanassa-javana) also produce laughter (hasana). The fire element (tejo-dhātu), known as cold or hot temperature (utu), produces temperature-born matter (utu-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa) internally and externally as appropriate, when it reaches the stage of presence (ṭhiti). Nutriment (āhāra) known as nutritive essence (ojā) produces nutriment-born matter (āhāra-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa) when it reaches the stage of presence at the time of being swallowed.
104: Among those groups of matter, the heart-base (hadaya-rūpa) and the eight faculties (indriya-rūpa) are born of kamma only. The two kinds of intimation (viññatti) are born of consciousness only. Sound (sadda) is born of consciousness and temperature. The three kinds of matter starting with lightness (lahutā) are born of temperature, consciousness, and nutriment. The eight kinds of inseparable matter (avinibbhoga-rūpa) and the space element (ākāsa-dhātu) are born of all four causes. The four characteristics of matter (lakkhaṇa-rūpa) are not born of any cause. 43. Kamma-born matter, consciousness-born matter, temperature-born matter, and nutriment-born matter are eighteen, fifteen, thirteen, and twelve respectively. 44. It is shown that the characteristics of matter are not born of any cause because they are merely the nature of the produced matter (nipphanna-rūpa) such as the arising and so forth. ## This is the Method of the Origins of Matter (Rūpasamuṭṭhānanaya) herein. 45. The twenty-one groups that have a common arising, a common cessation, a common dependence, and occur together are called material clusters (rūpa-kalāpa).
105:
There are eighteen, fifteen, thirteen, and twelve kinds respectively. Kamma-born matter, consciousness-born matter, temperature-born matter, and nutriment-born matter arise in order.

Because they are merely the nature of the produced matter (nipphanna-rūpa) such as the arising and so forth, it is shown that the four characteristics of matter are not born of any cause.

## This is the method of explaining the origins of matter in this Compendium of Matter (Rūpasaṅgaha).

## The Combination of Material Clusters

The twenty-one groups of matter that have a common arising, a common cessation, a common dependence, and occur together are called material clusters (rūpa-kalāpa).
106:
Among those twenty-one material clusters, the eight kinds of inseparable matter and the life-faculty (jīvita-rūpa) together with the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) are called the eye-decad (cakkhu-dasaka). Similarly, the ear-decad (sota-dasaka), nose-decad (ghāna-dasaka), tongue-decad (jivhā-dasaka), body-decad (kāya-dasaka), female-sex-decad (itthibhāva-dasaka), male-sex-decad (pumbhāva-dasaka), and heart-base-decad (vatthu-dasaka) should be combined in order.

The eight kinds of inseparable matter together with the life-faculty are called the life-nonad (jīvita-navaka). These nine material clusters are called kamma-born material clusters.

The eight kinds of inseparable matter are called the pure octad (suddhaṭṭhaka). That pure octad together with bodily intimation is the bodily-intimation-nonad (kāya-viññatti-navaka); together with vocal intimation and sound, it is the vocal-intimation-decad (vacī-viññatti-dasaka), ...
107:
...together with lightness and so forth, it is the lightness-undecad (lahutādiekādasaka); together with bodily intimation and lightness and so forth, it is the bodily-intimation-lightness-dodecad (kāya-viññatti-lahutādidvādassaka); together with vocal intimation, sound, and lightness and so forth, it is the vocal-intimation-sound-lightness-tredecad (vacī-viññatti-sadda-lahutāditayodassaka)—thus there are 6 consciousness-born material clusters.

The pure octad, the sound-nonad (sadda-navaka), the lightness-undecad, and the sound-lightness-dodecad (sadda-lahutādidvādassaka)—thus there are 4 temperature-born material clusters.

The pure octad and the lightness-undecad—thus there are 2 nutriment-born material clusters.

Among those material clusters, the two temperature-born material clusters called the pure octad and the sound-nonad are also found externally; all the remaining ones occur only in the internal continuity.
108:
The material clusters born of kamma, consciousness, temperature, and nutriment are nine, six, four, and two respectively, totaling twenty-one. Because the space element (ākāsa-dhātu) and the characteristics of matter (lakkhaṇa-rūpa) are the boundaries and markers of the clusters, the wise do not call them factors of the clusters.

## This is the Combination of Material Clusters in this Compendium of Matter.

## The Process of the Occurrence of Matter

All these kinds of matter are obtained in the sense-sphere (kāma-loka) during the course of existence (pavattikāla) as appropriate, without deficiency.
109: At the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), for moisture-born beings (saṃsedaja) and beings of spontaneous birth (opapātika), at the maximum, seven decads appear, namely the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, sex, and heart-base decads. At the minimum, however, the eye, ear, nose, and sex decads are sometimes not obtained; therefore, the deficiency of clusters should be understood by way of those decads. For womb-born beings (gabbhaseyyaka), three decads appear, namely the body, sex, and heart-base decads; even among those three, the sex-decad is sometimes not obtained. Thereafter, during the course of existence (pavattikāla), the eye-decad and so forth appear in order.
110:
In this way, starting from the arising (uppāda) of the rebirth-linking consciousness, the matter-groups produced by kamma arise; starting from the second consciousness, the matter-groups produced by consciousness arise; starting from the static phase (ṭhitikāla), the matter-groups produced by temperature (utu) arise; and starting from the time of the diffusion of nutritive essence (ojā), the matter-groups produced by nutriment arise. Thus, in the sense-sphere (kāmaloka), the continuity of matter-groups produced by these four causes proceeds uninterruptedly as long as life lasts, like the flame of a lamp or the current of a river.

At the time of death, however, starting from the static phase (ṭhitikāla) of the seventeenth consciousness counting backward from the death-consciousness (cuticitta), kamma-born matter no longer arises. Kamma-born matter that had arisen earlier continues to exist and ceases simultaneously with the death-consciousness. Thereafter, consciousness-born matter and nutriment-born matter also cease. Subsequently, the succession of matter-groups produced by temperature continues to occur as long as what is called the corpse (matakaḷevara) exists.
111:
In the manner just described,
Starting from the arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness in this life,
Just as the matter produced by the four causes occurs,
So too for deceased beings,
Starting from the arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness again in another existence,
The matter produced by the four causes occurs.

In the Fine-material Sphere (Rūpaloka), however, the nose-decad, tongue-decad, body-decad, sex-decad, and nutriment-born matter-groups are not found. Therefore, for those Fine-material Brahma beings, at the time of rebirth-linking, four kamma-produced matter-groups are found: the three decads by way of eye, ear, and base (vatthu), and the life-nonad. During the course of existence (pavatti), consciousness-born matter and temperature-born matter are also found.

For non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), however, the eye, ear, base, and sound are not found; likewise, all consciousness-born matter is not found. Therefore, for those non-percipient Brahma beings, at the time of rebirth-linking, only the life-nonad...
112:
...during the course of existence (pavatti), the temperature-produced matter, excluding sound-matter, remains and occurs.

Thus, the occurrence of matter should be understood in two ways—by way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence—in the three places known as the Sense-sphere, the Fine-material Sphere, and the Non-percipient Sphere.

In the 11 Sense-sphere planes, all 28 types of matter occur.
In the 15 Fine-material planes, 23 types of matter occur.
For non-percipient beings, only 17 types of matter occur.
In the 4 Formless planes, there is no matter at all.

Sound-matter, the 5 types of mutable matter (vikārarūpa), decay (jaratā), and
Impermanence (aniccatā) are not found at the time of rebirth-linking.
During the course of existence, however,
It is not that any matter is not found; indeed, they are all found.

## This is the process of the occurrence of matter in this Compendium of Matter.
113:
## Divisions of Nibbāna
Nibbāna is called a supramundane reality. It is to be realized by the four paths of Noble Knowledge (ariyamagga-ñāṇa) and is the object of the Paths and Fruits. It is called 'Nibbāna' because it is a departure from craving (taṇhā), which is called 'vāna' (weaving/attachment) because it binds beings to the round of rebirth (saṃsāra).

Although Nibbāna is onefold according to its nature, it is twofold according to the way it is categorized: the Nibbāna-element with the basis remaining (sa-upādisesa-nibbānadhātu) and the Nibbāna-element without the basis remaining (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). Furthermore, it is threefold according to its aspects: Void (suññata) Nibbāna, Signless (animitta) Nibbāna, and Desireless (appaṇihita) Nibbāna.

The Great Sages (Buddhas), who are free from the craving called 'vāna',
Declare the reality called Nibbāna,
Which is the deathless state, the ultimate end,
The unconditioned, and the unsurpassed.
114:
The Buddhas have clearly shown ultimate reality in four ways: consciousness, mental factors, matter, and Nibbāna.

## Thus ends the sixth chapter named the Compendium of Matter in the Abhidhammattha Sangaha.
115:
## 7. Samuccayasaṅgaha
I have already described the seventy-two kinds of entities (vatthudhamma)
Together with their respective functions and characteristics.
Now, I shall describe the compendium (samuccaya) of these realities
In their various categories as they appropriately apply.

The Compendium of Categories (Samuccayasaṅgaha) should be understood as fourfold: the Compendium of Evil (Akusalasaṅgaha), the Compendium of Mixed Categories (Missakasaṅgaha), the Compendium of the Requisites of Enlightenment (Bodhipakkhiyasaṅgaha), and the Compendium of the Whole (Sabbasaṅgaha).

## Compendium of Evil (Akusalasaṅgaha)
How is it to be understood? In the Compendium of Evil, first, there are four taints (āsava): the taint of sense-desire (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava).
116:
The four floods (ogha) are: the flood of sense-desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.
The four bonds (yoga) are: the bond of sense-desire, the bond of existence, the bond of views, and the bond of ignorance.
The four knots (gantha) are: the bodily knot of covetousness (abhijjhā-kāyagantha), the bodily knot of ill-will (byāpāda-kāyagantha), the bodily knot of adherence to rites and ceremonies (sīlabbata-parāmāsa-kāyagantha), and the bodily knot of dogmatic belief that 'This is the truth' (idaṃsaccābhinivesa-kāyagantha).
The four clingings (upādāna) are: clinging to sense-desire, clinging to views, clinging to rites and ceremonies, and clinging to a doctrine of self.
117:
The six hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are: the hindrance of sense-desire, the hindrance of ill-will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, the hindrance of doubt, and the hindrance of ignorance.
The seven latent tendencies (anusaya) are: the latent tendency to sensual lust, the latent tendency to lust for existence, the latent tendency to aversion, the latent tendency to conceit, the latent tendency to views, the latent tendency to doubt, and the latent tendency to ignorance.
According to the Suttanta method, the ten fetters (saṃyojana) are: the fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of lust for fine-material existence, the fetter of lust for formless existence, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of views, the fetter of adherence to rites and ceremonies, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of restlessness, and the fetter of ignorance.
118:
Another ten fetters as taught in the Abhidhamma (in the Vibhaṅga) are: the fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of lust for existence, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of views, the fetter of adherence to rites and ceremonies, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of envy, the fetter of stinginess, and the fetter of ignorance.

The ten defilements (kilesa) are: greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing.

To be specific, in this Compendium of Evil, among the taints and so forth, by the names 'sense-desire' (kāma) and 'existence' (bhava), craving (the mental factor of greed) which takes those as its objects is intended. Adherence to rites and ceremonies, the dogmatic belief that 'This is the truth', and clinging to a doctrine of self are simply different modes of the mental factor of views (diṭṭhi).
119:
In terms of ultimate realities (vatthuto), the taints, floods, and bonds are each threefold;
