The knots are also declared to be threefold.
The clingings are declared to be twofold,
And the hindrances are eightfold.

The latent tendencies are only six,
And the fetters are known to be nine.
The defilements are declared to be ten;
Thus, this Compendium of Evil is declared in nine ways.

## Compendium of Mixed Categories (Missakasaṅgaha)
In the Compendium of Mixed Categories, the six roots (hetu) are: greed, hatred, delusion, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.

The seven jhāna factors (jhānaṅga) are: initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), zest (pīti), one-pointedness (ekaggatā), joy (somanassa), displeasure (domanassa), and equanimity (upekkhā).
120:
The twelve path factors are: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, and wrong concentration.

The twenty-two faculties are: eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, female faculty, male faculty, life faculty, mind faculty, pleasure faculty, pain faculty, joy faculty, grief faculty, equanimity faculty, faith faculty, energy faculty, mindfulness faculty, concentration faculty, wisdom faculty, the faculty 'I shall come to know the unknown', the faculty of highest knowledge, and the faculty of one who has known.

The nine powers are: faith power, energy power, mindfulness power, concentration power, wisdom power—
121:
—shame power, fear of wrongdoing power, shamelessness power, and lack of fear of wrongdoing power.

The four predominants are: predominant desire, predominant energy, predominant consciousness, and predominant investigation.

The four nutriments are: edible food, contact as the second, mental volition as the third, and consciousness as the fourth.

Among the faculties in this Compendium of Mixed Categories, the knowledge of the path of stream-entry is called the faculty 'I shall come to know the unknown'. The knowledge of the fruit of Arahantship is called the faculty of one who has known. The six intermediate knowledges (the three higher paths and three lower fruits) are called the faculties of highest knowledge.
122:
The life faculty is also twofold by way of physical life faculty and mental life faculty.

In the ten types of sense-consciousness, the factors of absorption (jhāna) are not found; in the sixteen types of consciousness without energy, the powers (bala) are not found; in the eighteen types of rootless consciousness, the path factors (maggaṅga) are not found.

Likewise, in the consciousness accompanied by doubt, one-pointedness (ekaggatā) does not reach the state of a path factor, a faculty, or a power.

In the double-rooted and triple-rooted javanas, only one predominant is found at a time, as appropriate.

Six roots, five factors of absorption,
Nine path factors in terms of ultimate realities.
Sixteen faculty-phenomena,
And nine power-phenomena are declared.
Four predominants are stated,
Likewise four nutriments; thus in seven ways.
Interspersed with wholesome and other states,
The Compendium of Mixed Categories is declared.
123:
## Compendium of Enlightenment Factors (Bodhipakkhiya-sangaha)
In the Compendium of Enlightenment Factors, there are four foundations of mindfulness: the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness of consciousness, and the foundation of mindfulness of mental objects.

There are four right efforts: the effort to abandon arisen unwholesome states, the effort to prevent the arising of unarisen unwholesome states, the effort to arouse unarisen wholesome states, and the effort to further increase arisen wholesome states.

There are four bases of power: the base of power of desire, the base of power of energy, the base of power of consciousness, and the base of power of investigation.
124:
The five faculties are: faith faculty, energy faculty, mindfulness faculty, concentration faculty, and wisdom faculty.

The five powers are: faith power, energy power, mindfulness power, concentration power, and wisdom power.

The seven factors of enlightenment are: mindfulness enlightenment factor, investigation of phenomena enlightenment factor, energy enlightenment factor, joy enlightenment factor, tranquility enlightenment factor, concentration enlightenment factor, and equanimity enlightenment factor.

The eight path factors are: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
125:
In this Compendium of Enlightenment Factors, the single factor of right mindfulness is declared as the four foundations of mindfulness.

Likewise, the single factor of right effort is declared as the four right efforts.

Desire, consciousness, equanimity,
Faith, tranquility, joy,
Right view, intention,
Effort, the three abstinences,
Right mindfulness, and concentration—
These phenomena are fourteen in terms of their nature.
By way of thirty-seven variations,
There is a compendium of seven groups therein.

Intention, tranquility, joy, equanimity,
Desire, consciousness, and the three abstinences—
These nine phenomena are established in one place each; energy is established in nine places;
Mindfulness is established in eight places; concentration in four places; and wisdom in five places.
126:
Faith is established in two places. Thus ends the noble classification of the thirty-seven supreme enlightenment factors.

All enlightenment factors occur in supramundane consciousness. In some supramundane consciousness, initial application (vitakka) and joy (pīti) do not occur. In mundane beautiful consciousness, they occur as appropriate in the occurrence of the six purifications.

## Compendium of All (Sabba-sangaha)
In the Compendium of All, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of matter, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.

The five aggregates of clinging are: the aggregate of matter-clinging, the aggregate of feeling-clinging, the aggregate of perception-clinging, the aggregate of mental formations-clinging, and the aggregate of consciousness-clinging.
127:
The twelve bases are: eye base, ear base, nose base, tongue base, body base, mind base, visible form base, sound base, smell base, taste base, tangible object base, and mental object base.

The eighteen elements are: eye element, ear element, nose element, tongue element, body element, visible form element, sound element, smell element, taste element, tangible object element, eye-consciousness element, ear-consciousness element, nose-consciousness element, tongue-consciousness element, body-consciousness element, mind element, mental object element, and mind-consciousness element.

The four Noble Truths are: the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, ...
128:
...the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

In this Compendium of All, sixty-nine phenomena consisting of mental factors, subtle matter, and Nibbāna are known as the mental object base and the mental object element.

The mind base alone is divided by way of the seven consciousness elements.

Matter, feeling, perception,
Likewise the remaining mental factors,
And consciousness—these five
Are declared as the five aggregates.

Likewise, those belonging to the three planes
Are known as the five aggregates of clinging.

Because of the absence of division, Nibbāna
Is excluded from the classification of aggregates.
129:
The sense bases are twelvefold by way of doors and objects. The elements are eighteenfold by way of doors, objects, and the consciousnesses arising dependent on those doors and objects.

The truth of suffering is the round of existence occurring in the three planes; craving is the truth of the origin. Nibbāna is called the truth of cessation; the supramundane eightfold path is known as the truth of the path.

The states associated with the path and the fruition states are excluded from the four truths. Thus, the Compendium of All is stated in five ways.

## Thus ends the seventh chapter named the Compendium of Categories in the Abhidhammattha Sangaha.
130:
## 8. Compendium of Relations
I shall now explain, as is fitting, the distinctions of those conditioned states, which states are conditions for which states, and in what way. The Compendium of Relations (Paccaya-sangaha) should be understood as twofold: the method of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda-naya) and the method of Conditional Relations (Paṭṭhāna-naya). Therein, the method of Dependent Origination is marked by the mere mode of the arising of effects, such as volitional formations, through the existence of causes, such as ignorance. The method of Conditional Relations is stated with reference to the specific conditionality. The teachers explain by combining both.
131:
## The Method of Dependent Origination
Therein, dependent on ignorance (avijjā), volitional formations (saṅkhāra) arise. Dependent on volitional formations, consciousness (viññāṇa) arises. Dependent on consciousness, mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) arises. Dependent on mentality-materiality, the sixfold sense base (saḷāyatana) arises. Dependent on the sixfold sense base, contact (phassa) arises. Dependent on contact, feeling (vedanā) arises. Dependent on feeling, craving (taṇhā) arises. Dependent on craving, clinging (upādāna) arises. Dependent on clinging, existence (bhava) arises. Dependent on existence, birth (jāti) arises. Dependent on birth, aging (jarā), death (maraṇa), sorrow (soka), lamentation (parideva), pain (dukkha), grief (domanassa), and despair (upāyāsa) arise. Thus is the arising of this entire mass of suffering, which is unmixed with happiness, through this sequence of conditions. This is the method of Dependent Origination.

In this method of Dependent Origination, three periods, twelve factors, twenty modes, three connections, four groups, three rounds, and two roots should be understood.
132:
How should they be understood? Ignorance and volitional formations are called the past period. Birth, aging, and death are called the future period. The eight factors in the middle (consciousness, mentality-materiality, the sixfold sense base, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, and existence) are called the present period. Thus there are three periods.

There are twelve factors: ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, mentality-materiality, the sixfold sense base, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and aging-death.

In this method of Dependent Origination, the mention of sorrow and so forth is intended only to show the incidental consequences of birth.

Among these twelve factors, by taking ignorance and volitional formations, craving, clinging, and existence are also taken. Likewise, by taking craving, clinging, and existence—
133:
(Just as by taking ignorance and volitional formations, craving, clinging, and existence are taken), by taking birth, aging, and death, the pentad of effects beginning with consciousness is also taken. Thus:

Five causes were in the past,
Five effects are in the present.
Five causes are in the present,
Five effects will be in the future.

Thus there are twenty modes, three connections, and four groups.

Ignorance, craving, and clinging are the round of defilements (kilesa-vaṭṭa). Volitional formations and the part of existence called kamma-existence (kamma-bhava) are the round of kamma (kamma-vaṭṭa). The part of existence called rebirth-existence (upapatti-bhava) and the remaining factors (consciousness, mentality-materiality, the sixfold sense base, contact, feeling, birth, aging, and death) are the round of resultants (vipāka-vaṭṭa). Thus there are three rounds.
134:
Two roots should also be understood by way of ignorance and craving.

Through the total cessation of these two roots (ignorance and craving), the round of existence ceases. For beings who are constantly oppressed by aging, death, and delusion, ignorance arises due to the arising of taints (āsava). In this way, the Great Sage taught Dependent Origination as the arising of effects dependent on the concurrence of causes—the beginningless round of existence occurring in the three planes.

## The Method of Conditional Relations
Root condition, object condition, predominance condition, proximity condition—
135:
contiguity condition, conascence condition, mutuality condition, dependence condition, decisive dependence condition, pre-existence condition, post-existence condition, repetition condition, kamma condition, resultant condition, nutriment condition, faculty condition, jhāna condition, path condition, association condition, dissociation condition, presence condition, absence condition, disappearance condition, and non-disappearance condition. This is the method of Conditional Relations.

Mentality is a condition for mentality in six ways.

For mentality-materiality in five ways.

Again, for materiality in one way.

Materiality is a condition for mentality in one way.

Concepts, mentality, and materiality are conditions for mentality in two ways.

Mentality-materiality is a condition for mentality-materiality in nine ways. In what way are the conditions established in these six groups?
136:
Mental states (consciousness and mental factors) that have just ceased are conditions for the present mental states by way of proximity, contiguity, absence, and disappearance. Preceding javanas are conditions for subsequent javanas by way of repetition. Conascent mental states are conditions for each other by way of association. Thus, mentality is a condition for mentality in six ways.

Roots, jhāna factors, and path factors are conditions for conascent mentality-materiality by way of root condition, etc. Conascent volition is a condition for conascent mentality-materiality, and volition at different moments is a condition for mentality-materiality produced by kamma by way of kamma condition. Resultant aggregates are conditions for each other and for conascent materiality by way of resultant condition. Thus, mentality is a condition for mentality-materiality in five ways.
137:
The mental states of consciousness and mental factors that arise later are a condition for this body that arose earlier by way of post-nascent (pacchājāta) condition. In this single way, mind (nāma) is a condition for matter (rūpa).

The six bases are conditions for the seven consciousness elements during the course of existence (pavatti), and the five objects are conditions for the five-fold consciousness process by way of pre-nascent (purejāta) condition. In this single way, matter is a condition for mind.

Concepts (paññatti), mind, and matter are conditions for mind only, in two ways: by way of object (ārammaṇa) and by way of strong dependence (upanissaya).

Among those two, the object is of six kinds by way of visible form and so forth.

Strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya) is of three kinds: object strong dependence (ārammaṇūpanissaya)...
138: proximity strong dependence (anantarūpanissaya) and natural strong dependence (pakatūpanissaya). Among those three, only the object that is highly esteemed is the object strong dependence condition. The mental states of consciousness and mental factors that have just ceased in proximity are the proximity strong dependence condition. However, states such as lust (rāga) and so forth, states such as faith (saddhā) and so forth, happiness, suffering, the person, food, climate, and lodgings—as is appropriate, whether internal or external—are conditions for wholesome states and so forth; and kamma is a condition for its results (vipāka). Thus, natural strong dependence is of many kinds. By way of predominance (adhipati), co-nascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), dependence (nissaya), nutriment (āhāra), faculty (indriya), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata), mind and matter are conditions for mind and matter in nine ways as is appropriate.
139:
Among those nine conditions, the predominant object is a condition for mental states by way of object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati). The fourfold co-nascent predominance is a condition for co-nascent mind and matter by way of co-nascence. Thus, the predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya) is of two kinds.

The mental states of consciousness and mental factors are conditions for one another and for co-nascent matter (mind-produced matter and rebirth-kamma-produced matter). The great essentials (mahābhūta) are conditions for one another and for derived matter (upādā-rūpa). At the moment of rebirth-linking, the heart-base and the resultant mental aggregates are conditions for one another. Thus, the co-nascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya) is of three kinds.

The mental states of consciousness and mental factors are conditions for one another. The great essentials are conditions for one another. At the moment of rebirth-linking, the heart-base and the resultant mental aggregates are conditions for one another. Thus, the mutuality condition (aññamañña-paccaya) is of three kinds.

The mental states of consciousness and mental factors are conditions for one another and for co-nascent matter (mind-produced matter and rebirth-kamma-produced matter). The great essentials are conditions for one another and for derived matter. The six bases are conditions for the seven consciousness elements. Thus, the dependence condition (nissaya-paccaya) is of three kinds.
140: The nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya) is of two kinds: (1) physical food (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra) which is a condition for this body, and (2) mental nutriments (contact, volition, consciousness) which are conditions for the co-nascent mind and matter. The faculty condition (indriya-paccaya) is of three kinds: (1) the five sensitive materialities (pasāda-rūpa) which are conditions for the five consciousnesses, (2) the material life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) which is a condition for kamma-produced matter, and (3) the mental faculties which are conditions for the co-nascent mind and matter. The dissociation condition (vippayutta-paccaya) is of three kinds: (1) at the moment of descent (rebirth), the heart-base is a condition for resultant mental aggregates, and consciousness and mental factors are conditions for co-nascent matter by way of co-nascence (sahajāta); (2) the mental states of consciousness and mental factors that arise later are conditions for this body that arose earlier by way of post-nascent (pacchājāta) condition; and (3) during the course of existence, the six bases are conditions for the seven consciousness elements by way of pre-nascent (purejāta) condition. Co-nascence, pre-nascence, post-nascence, physical food, and material life-faculty (are all types of the presence condition).
141: The presence condition (atthi-paccaya) and the non-disappearance condition (avigata-paccaya) are each of five kinds. In the conditions of object, strong dependence, kamma, and presence, all other conditions are included and converge. Herein, co-nascent matter (sahajāta-rūpa) should be understood as being of two kinds: mind-produced matter during the whole course of existence and kamma-produced matter at the moment of rebirth-linking. Thus, the states belonging to the three periods of time, those that are beyond time, internal states, external states, as well as conditioned and unconditioned states, exist in three ways by way of concept (paññatti), mind (nāma), and matter (rūpa). In the Great Book of Patthana, there are twenty-four conditions in all. Among those (concept, mind, and matter), the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) is called matter. The four mental aggregates, namely consciousness and mental factors, together with Nibbāna—these five are called the immaterial (arūpa) or mind (nāma). Concept (paññatti), which is distinct from mind and matter, is of two kinds: concept as meaning (atthapaññatti) because it is that which is made known, and concept as sound/name (saddapaññatti) because it is that which makes known. How? Based on the mode of change in the respective great essentials, there are concepts such as land, mountains, and so forth; based on the mode of composition of materials, there are concepts such as house, chariot, cart, and so forth...
142:
Among those concepts, mind, and matter, only the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) is specifically called matter. The four mental aggregates, known as consciousness and mental factors, and Nibbāna—these five kinds of states are specifically called the immaterial (arūpa) or mind (nāma).

## Classification of Concepts (Paññattibheda)
Concept (paññatti), which is distinct from mind and matter, is of two kinds: concept as meaning (atthapaññatti) because it is that which is made known, and concept as sound/name (saddapaññatti) because it is that which makes known.

How is this so? Based on the mode of change in the respective great essentials like earth and so forth, there are concepts of shape (saṇṭhāna-paññatti) such as land and mountains, which are made known in those respective ways. Based on the mode of composition of materials such as wood, lumps of earth, and thread, there are collective concepts (samūha-paññatti) such as house, chariot, and cart, which are made known in those respective ways. Based on the five aggregates, there are concepts of class (jātipaññatti) such as man and person, which are made known in those respective ways. Based on the mode of the moon, sun, and constellations revolving clockwise around Mount Meru, there are concepts such as direction and time, which are made known in those respective ways—
143:
Based on the aspect of non-contact such as holes and caves, the space-concepts (ākāsa-paññatti) are made known in various ways. Based on the signs of the earth-kasiṇa and the specific progression of meditation, the kasiṇa-concepts (kasiṇa-paññatti) are made known in various ways, and so forth. Although these concepts do not exist in the ultimate sense, they become objects of consciousness and mental factors in the form of a shadow of the meaning. Being conceived, depending on, and by means of those respective aspects, they are reckoned, designated, termed, and made known in various ways. Therefore, they are called 'concepts' (paññatti). This concept is called 'concept of meaning' (attha-paññatti) because it is that which is made known.

Because it is that which makes known, the concept of sound (sadda-paññatti) is shown by names such as 'nāma' and 'nāmakamma'. That concept of sound has six varieties: concept of the existent, concept of the non-existent, concept of the non-existent by the existent, —

42. Among those six, when things that exist in the ultimate sense, such as matter (rūpa) and feeling (vedanā), are made known by this sound, then this sound is called 'concept of the existent' (vijjamāna-paññatti).
144:
—concept of the existent by the non-existent, concept of the existent by the existent, and concept of the non-existent by the non-existent; thus there are six varieties.

Among those six kinds of concepts, when things that exist in the ultimate sense, such as matter (rūpa) and feeling (vedanā), are made known by this (concept of sound), then this concept is called 'concept of the existent' (vijjamāna-paññatti). When things that do not exist in the ultimate sense, such as land and mountains, are made known by this (concept of sound), then this concept is called 'concept of the non-existent' (avijjamāna-paññatti). The remaining (four) should be understood by way of mixing the two, respectively: 'one with six supernormal powers' (chaḷabhiñño), 'woman's voice' (itthisaddo), 'eye-consciousness' (cakkhuviññāṇaṃ), and 'king's son' (rājaputto).

Following the sequence of vocal sounds,
In the (sequence of) the ear-consciousness process,
Occurring immediately thereafter,
They are objects of the mind-door process.
145:
Following the sequence of that (concept of name),
The concepts of meaning are understood thereafter.
That concept of name, created by worldly convention and symbols,
Should be understood.

## Thus ends the Eighth Chapter, titled the Analysis of the Compendium of Relations,
## in the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha.
146:
## 9. Kammaṭṭhāna-pariccheda (Section on Meditation Subjects)

After this Compendium of Relations,
I shall speak of the two-fold meditation subjects,
Namely Tranquillity (Samatha) and Insight (Vipassanā),
In their respective order.

## Samatha-kammaṭṭhāna

Among those two, Tranquillity and Insight, in the Compendium of Tranquillity, first, the Compendium of Tranquillity Meditation Subjects should be understood in seven ways: ten kasiṇas, ten foulness (asubha), ten recollections (anussati), four illimitables (appamaññā), one perception (saññā), one analysis (vavatthāna), and four immaterial spheres (āruppa).

## Varieties of Temperament

Lustful temperament, hateful temperament, deluded temperament, faithful temperament, intelligent temperament —
147:
— and discursive temperament; thus the Compendium of Temperaments should be understood in six ways.

## Varieties of Development

Preliminary development (parikamma-bhāvanā), access development (upacāra-bhāvanā), and absorption development (appanā-bhāvanā)—these three kinds of development should be understood.

## Varieties of Signs

Preliminary sign (parikamma-nimitta), learning sign (uggaha-nimitta), and counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta)—these three kinds of signs should also be understood.

How? Earth-kasiṇa, water-kasiṇa, fire-kasiṇa, air-kasiṇa, blue-kasiṇa, yellow-kasiṇa, red-kasiṇa, white-kasiṇa, space-kasiṇa, and light-kasiṇa—these ten are called the ten kasiṇas.
148:
Bloated (corpse), livid, festering, cut-up, gnawed, scattered, hacked and scattered, blood-stained, worm-infested, and skeleton—these ten are called the foulness (asubha).

Recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati), recollection of the Dhamma (Dhammānussati), recollection of the Saṅgha (Saṅghānussati), recollection of virtue (Sīlānussati), recollection of generosity (Cāgānussati), recollection of deities (Devatānussati), recollection of peace (Upasamānussati), recollection of death (Maraṇānussati), mindfulness occupied with the body (Kāyagatāsati), and mindfulness of breathing (Ānāpānassati)—these ten are called the recollections (anussati).

Loving-kindness (Mettā), compassion (Karuṇā), appreciative joy (Muditā), and equanimity (Upekkhā)—these four are called the illimitables (appamaññā); they are also termed the divine abodes (brahmavihāra).
149:
The perception of repulsiveness in food (āhārepaṭikūlasaññā) is the one perception.

The analysis of the four elements (catudhātuvavatthāna) is the one analysis.

The four starting with the sphere of infinite space are called the immaterial spheres (āruppa). Thus, in every way, there are forty meditation subjects in the exposition of tranquillity.

## Analysis of Meditation Subjects by Temperament

To speak specifically, among the six temperaments, the ten foulness and the meditation on the parts of the body called mindfulness occupied with the body are suitable for one of lustful temperament.
150:
The four illimitables and the four kasinas, such as blue and so forth, are suitable for one of hateful temperament. Mindfulness of breathing is suitable for one of deluded temperament and one of discursive temperament. The six recollections, such as the recollection of the Buddha and so forth, are suitable for one of faithful temperament. Recollection of death, recollection of peace, the perception of repulsiveness in food, and the analysis of the four elements are suitable for one of intelligent temperament. All the remaining meditation subjects are suitable for all temperaments. Among them, in the case of kasinas, a large kasina disk is suitable for one of deluded temperament, while a small kasina disk is suitable only for one of discursive temperament.

## This is the distinction of suitability.

## Distinction of Development
Among the developments, preliminary development is obtained in all meditation subjects.
151:
In these ten meditation subjects—namely, the eight recollections beginning with the recollection of the Buddha, the perception of repulsiveness in food, and the analysis of the four elements—only access concentration is attained; there is no absorption. In the remaining thirty meditation subjects, absorption concentration is also attained. Among those meditation subjects that lead to absorption, the ten kasinas and mindfulness of breathing are meditation subjects that can lead to all five jhānas. The ten foulness subjects and mindfulness occupied with the body are meditation subjects that lead only to the first jhāna. The three divine abodes, such as loving-kindness and so forth, are meditation subjects that lead to the four jhānas. The divine abode of equanimity is a meditation subject that leads to the fifth jhāna. Thus, twenty-six meditation subjects lead to the fine-material sphere jhānas. The four immaterial states lead to the immaterial sphere jhānas.

## This is the distinction of development.
152:
## Distinction of Objects (Gocarabheda)
Among the signs, the preliminary sign (parikamma-nimitta) and the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) can be obtained in all meditation subjects as appropriate and in a figurative sense.

The counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta), however, can be obtained only in the kasiṇas, foulness (asubha), the parts of the body (koṭṭhāsa/kāyagatāsati), and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati). In these meditation subjects, access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) arise based on the counterpart sign.

How? For a beginner who is grasping the sign in the earth disk and so forth, that object is called the preliminary sign (parikamma-nimitta). That development is called preliminary development (parikamma-bhāvanā).

When that sign is well-grasped by the mind, just as if one were seeing it with the eyes...
153:
...and comes into the range of the mind-door, then that very object is called the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta). And that development becomes concentrated.

For the meditator who is thus concentrated, when he subsequently applies himself to development by means of preliminary concentration (parikamma-samādhi) on that learning sign, and when an object born of development, which is similar to that [learning sign] but free from the physical thing (or free from the flaws of the kasiṇa), and which is called a concept (paññatti), becomes well-settled and fixed in the mind, then it is said that the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) has arisen.

From that point onwards, access development (upacāra-bhāvanā), which is called sense-sphere concentration (kāmāvacara-samādhi) and is free from the obstacles of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), is said to be accomplished.

Thereafter, for the meditator who practices well with that very counterpart sign by means of access concentration, the first fine-material sphere jhana (rūpāvacara-paṭhama-jhāna) arises by way of absorption (appanā).
154:
Thereafter, having mastered that very first jhana through these five masteries—adverting, attaining, resolving, emerging, and reviewing—for the sake of abandoning the gross jhana factors such as initial application (vitakka) and for the sake of the arising of subtle jhana factors such as sustained application (vicāra), for the meditator who strives, the second jhana and so forth reach absorption in due order as appropriate.

In this way, the counterpart sign is obtained in twenty-two meditation subjects, such as the earth kasiṇa.

Among the remaining meditation subjects, the limitless states (appamaññā) occur in the concept of beings (satta-paññatti).

Among the kasiṇas, excluding the space kasiṇa, for one who performs the preliminary work by meditating on the space obtained by removing any one of the kasiṇas as infinite, the first immaterial jhana reaches absorption.
155:
For one who performs the preliminary work by meditating on that very first immaterial jhana consciousness as infinite, the second immaterial jhana reaches absorption.

For one who performs the preliminary work on the absence of that first immaterial jhana consciousness as "there is nothing," the third immaterial jhana reaches absorption.

For one who performs the preliminary work on the third immaterial jhana as "this is peaceful, this is sublime," the fourth immaterial jhana reaches absorption.

In the remaining ten meditation subjects, having performed the preliminary work by taking an object such as the virtues of the Buddha, when that sign is well-grasped, the preliminary development (parikamma-bhāvanā) becomes concentrated in that very object, and access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) is accomplished.

However, for the fine-material sphere fifth jhana occurring by the power of direct knowledge (abhiññā), for one who emerges from the fifth jhana which is the basis for direct knowledge, adverts to the resolution and so forth, and performs the preliminary work...
156:
...the fine-material sphere fifth jhana occurring by the power of direct knowledge arises in objects such as visible forms through absorption as appropriate.

Direct knowledge (Abhiññā) is of five kinds:
1. The power of supernormal feats (iddhividha),
2. The divine ear (dibbasota),
3. Knowledge of the minds of others (paracittavijānana),
4. Recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati),
5. The divine eye (dibbacakkhu).

## This which has been stated is the distinction of objects in this Samatha meditation.
## The method of Samatha meditation is finished.
## Vipassanā Meditation
## Distinction of Purifications (Visuddhibheda)

In Vipassanā meditation, the collection of purifications (visuddhi) should be understood in seven ways: purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi), purification of mind (citta-visuddhi), purification of view (diṭṭhi-visuddhi), purification by overcoming doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-visuddhi), purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path (maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi), purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi), and purification by knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana-visuddhi).
157:
There are three characteristics: the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa), the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa), and the characteristic of non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa).

There are three contemplations: contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), and contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā).

There are ten insight knowledges (vipassanā-ñāṇa): knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa), knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbaya-ñāṇa), knowledge of dissolution (bhaṅga-ñāṇa), knowledge of fear (bhaya-ñāṇa), knowledge of danger (ādīnava-ñāṇa), knowledge of disenchantment (nibbidā-ñāṇa), knowledge of desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa), knowledge of reflective contemplation (paṭisaṅkhā-ñāṇa), knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa), and conformity knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa).

There are three liberations (vimokkha): emptiness liberation (suññata-vimokkha), signless liberation (animitta-vimokkha), and desireless liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha).
158:
Three doors to liberation (vimokkhamukha) should also be known: contemplation of emptiness (suññatānupassanā), contemplation of the signless (animittānupassanā), and contemplation of the desireless (appaṇihitānupassanā).

How? The fourfold purification of virtue—virtue regarding restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla), virtue regarding restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara-sīla), virtue regarding purification of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla), and virtue regarding the use of requisites (paccayasannissita-sīla)—is called purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi).

Both kinds of concentration—access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi)—are called purification of mind (citta-visuddhi).

The discerning of mentality and materiality (nāmarūpa-pariggaha) by way of characteristic (lakkhaṇa), function (rasa), manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna), and proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) is called purification of view (diṭṭhi-visuddhi).
159: The discernment of the causes of those very mental and material phenomena is called Purification by Overcoming Doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi). Thereafter, for one who contemplates the three characteristics by means of the knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa)—summarizing by way of groups (kalāpa) the formations (saṅkhāra) of the three planes, which have been thus discerned with their causes and which are divided into past, etc., according to the methods of the aggregates (khandha), etc., as: "It is impermanent (anicca) in the sense of being subject to destruction; it is suffering (dukkha) in the sense of being fearful; it is non-self (anattā) in the sense of being coreless"—by way of duration, continuity, or the moment; and for one who repeatedly perceives the rise and fall by means of the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) in those very formations by way of cause and by way of the moment: "Effulgence (obhāsa), rapture (pīti), tranquility (passaddhi), resolution (adhimokkha), exertion (paggaha), happiness (sukha), knowledge (ñāṇa), presence of mindfulness (upaṭṭhāna), equanimity (upekkhā), and attachment (nikanti)" (arise).
160:
The determination of the characteristics of what is the path and what is not the path, by way of discerning the ten imperfections of insight such as effulgence (obhāsa), is called Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What is Path and Not-Path (maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi).

Likewise, for that person who is free from those imperfections, the nine insight knowledges from the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) up to the knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa), as he practices the sequence of insight into the three characteristics, are called Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way (paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi).

For that person practicing in this way, based on the maturation of insight knowledge, thinking "Now the absorption (appanā) will arise," the stream of subconsciousness (bhavaṅga) is interrupted. Immediately after the arising of the mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana), two or three insight-consciousnesses occur under the names of preparatory (parikamma), access (upacāra), and conformity (anuloma), taking as their object any one of the characteristics such as impermanence.

That knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa) together with the knowledge of conformity which has reached its peak is also called insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā).
161:
There exists that knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa) which has reached the peak of insight; that knowledge of equanimity towards formations together with the knowledge of conformity to the truths is also called, in another way, insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā).

After that impulse-moment of insight leading to emergence, the change-of-lineage consciousness (gotrabhū) arises, taking Nibbāna as its object, overcoming the lineage of worldlings (puthujjana) and reaching the lineage of the noble ones (ariya).

Immediately after that change-of-lineage consciousness, the Path (magga) enters the absorption process (appanā-vīthi) by way of developing the truth of the path (magga-sacca), while fully understanding the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca), abandoning the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca), and realizing the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca).

After that, two or three moments of fruition consciousness (phala-citta) occur, and then there is the lapse into the stream of subconsciousness (bhavaṅga).

Then, interrupting the stream of subconsciousness, the knowledges of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) arise.
162:
The wise noble one reviews the Path, the Fruit, and Nibbāna. He may or may not review the defilements that have been abandoned and the defilements that remain.

In this way, according to the sequence of the six purifications, the fourfold Path that is to be developed is called, in another way, Purification by Knowledge and Vision (ñāṇadassanavisuddhi).

## This is the differentiation of purifications herein.

## Differentiation of Liberations

Among those insights, the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā), which abandons the firm adherence to a self (attā), is the door to liberation (vimokkhamukha) called contemplation of emptiness (suññatānupassanā).

The contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), which abandons the sign of perversion (vipallāsa-nimitta), is called contemplation of the signless (animittānupassanā).
163:
The contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā) is called contemplation of the desireless (appaṇihitānupassanā) because it abandons the longing of craving (taṇhā).

Therefore, if insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) contemplates as non-self, the Path is called the 'empty liberation' (suññata-vimokkha). If it contemplates as impermanent, the Path is called the 'signless liberation' (animitta-vimokkha). If it contemplates as suffering, the Path is called the 'desireless liberation' (appaṇihita-vimokkha). Thus, the Path receives three names by way of the insight that leads to it. Likewise, in the Path-process, the Fruit (phala) also receives three names by way of the Path that leads to it.

However, in the process of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti-vīthi), for those contemplating in the aforementioned manner, even though their respective fruition arises, it is called 'empty liberation', etc., only by way of the insight that leads to it. But by way of the object and by way of its own nature (sarasa), all three names are the same for all Paths and Fruits in all places.

## This is the differentiation of liberations herein.
164: ## Differentiation of Individuals (puggalabhedo). In this insight meditation, one who has developed the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) and has abandoned the journey to the woeful states by abandoning wrong view (diṭṭhi) and doubt (vicikicchā), and who is limited to seven more births at most in the human and celestial realms, is called a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna). One who has developed the Path of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga) and has attenuated lust (rāga), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha), and returns to this world only once, is called a Once-returner (sakadāgāmī). One who has developed the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga) and has completely abandoned sensual lust (kāmarāga) and ill-will (byāpāda), and does not return to this sensual plane again, is called a Non-returner (anāgāmī). One who has developed the Path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga) and has completely abandoned all defilements is called an Arahant—
165:
...he becomes an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, worthy of the highest offerings in the world.

## This is the distinction of individuals.

## Distinction of Attainments
In this context of the development of insight, the cognitive process of the attainment of fruition is common to all noble ones according to their respective fruition. However, the attainment of cessation is attained only by Non-returners and Arahants. In that attainment of cessation, one enters the sublime attainments in succession, beginning with the first jhāna; after emerging from each, one contemplates with insight the conditioned states occurring therein. Having proceeded thus up to the sphere of nothingness and having performed the preliminary duties such as the resolution and so forth, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. After two moments of absorption impulsions for that person, the stream of consciousness is cut off. After the stream of consciousness is thus cut off, one is said to have entered the attainment of cessation.
166:
For that Non-returner or Arahant, after the two moments of wholesome or functional impulse-consciousness of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the continuity of consciousness is interrupted. Due to this interruption of the continuity of consciousness, he is said to have entered the attainment of cessation.

At the time of emerging from the attainment of cessation, for a Non-returner, the fruition consciousness of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala-citta) occurs once, and for an Arahant, the fruition consciousness of Arahatship (arahatta-phala-citta) occurs once, and then there is the lapse into the stream of subconsciousness (bhavaṅga). After that lapse into the stream of subconsciousness, the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) arises.

## This is the differentiation of attainments in this section.

## The method of insight meditation is concluded.

## Exhortation

One who desires the taste of the practice (the bliss of jhāna and fruition) in the Dispensation should thus develop these two supreme meditations (samatha and vipassanā).

## Thus ends the ninth chapter called the Compendium of Meditation Subjects (kammaṭṭhāna-saṅgaha-vibhāga) in the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha.
167:
## Conclusion

(a) The donor named Nampa, born of a noble family distinguished by conduct and possessing pure qualities of greatly increased faith, requested this work out of compassion for others. That work [the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha] is now completed.

(b) By the extensive merit of composing this work, may the conscientious monks, adorned with the pure qualities of wisdom, in the very famous Mūlasoma monastery—the abode of the fortunate—regard this for the blessing of the increase of merit and prosperity.

## Thus is finished the work named Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha, composed by the teacher Anuruddha.
